Batch inference with Gemini

To see an example of using batch inference, run the "Intro to Batch Predictions with the Gemini API" notebook in one of the following environments:

Open in Colab | Open in Colab Enterprise | Open in Agent Platform Workbench | View on GitHub

Get asynchronous, high-throughput, and cost-effective inference for your large-scale data processing needs with Gemini's batch inference (formerly known as batch prediction). This guide walks you through the value of batch inference, how it works, its limitations, and best practices for optimal results.

Why use batch inference?

In many real-world scenarios, you don't need an immediate response from a language model. Instead, you might have a large dataset of prompts that you need to process efficiently and affordably. This is where batch inference shines.

Key benefits include:

  • Cost-Effectiveness: Batch processing is offered at a 50% discounted rate compared to real-time inference, making it ideal for large-scale, non-urgent tasks. Implicit caching is enabled by default for Gemini 2.5 and later models, providing a 90% discount on cached input tokens compared to standard input tokens:

    • Gemini 3 and later models: For supported models, the cache and batch discounts stack, providing a 95% total discount on cached input tokens compared to standard input tokens.
    • Gemini 2.5 models: The discounts for cache and batch don't stack. The 90% cache hit discount takes precedence over the batch discount.

    For model-specific rates, see Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform pricing.

  • High rate limits: Process hundreds of thousands of requests in a single batch with a higher rate limit compared to the real-time Gemini API.

  • Simplified Workflow: Instead of managing a complex pipeline of individual real-time requests, you can submit a single batch job and retrieve the results once the processing is complete. The service handles format validation, parallelizes requests for concurrent processing, and automatically retries to strive for a high completion rate with 24 hours turnaround time.

Batch inference is optimized for large-scale processing tasks like:

  • Content Generation: Generate product descriptions, social media posts, or other creative text in bulk.
  • Data Annotation and Classification: Classify user reviews, categorize documents, or perform sentiment analysis on a large corpus of text.
  • Offline Analysis: Summarize articles, extract key information from reports, or translate documents at scale.
  • Embedding Generation: Generate vector embeddings for a large document corpus to power semantic search, retrieval, and clustering workloads.

Gemini models that support batch inference

The following base and tuned Gemini models support batch inference:

Note: Batch inference is not supported for tuned Gemini 3 and later models.

Click to expand supported models

Embedding models that support batch inference

Batch inference is also available for embedding models:

  • Gemini embedding models (Preview): gemini-embedding-001 and gemini-embedding-2. Each batch job supports up to 1,000,000 rows, and each project supports up to 10,000 concurrent batch jobs in the queue.
  • Legacy text embedding models: all stable versions, including text-embedding-004, text-embedding-005, and text-multilingual-embedding-002. Each request can include up to 30,000 prompts.

Embedding batch jobs use a different input and output schema than Gemini text generation batch jobs, and the request limits in Quotas and limits don't apply to them. For the required JSONL schema, per-model configuration options, and examples, see Get batch embeddings inferences.

Global endpoint model support

Batch inference supports using the global endpoint for base Gemini models. It doesn't support the global endpoint for tuned Gemini models.

The global endpoint helps improve overall availability by serving your requests from any region that's supported by the model that you're using. Note that it doesn't support data residency requirements. If you have data residency requirements, use the regional endpoints.

Quotas and limits

While batch inference is powerful, it's important to be aware of the following limitations.

  • Quota: There are no predefined quota limits on your usage. Instead, batch service provides access to a large, shared pool of resources, dynamically allocated based on availability of resources and real-time demand across all customers of that model. When more customers are active and our capacity is saturated, your batch requests might be queued for capacity.
  • Queue Time: When our service experiences high traffic, your batch job will queue for capacity. The job remains in queue for up to 72 hours before it expires.
  • Request Limits: A single batch job may include up to 200,000 requests. If you are using Cloud Storage as input, there is also a file size limit of 1GB. Embedding models have different request limits. For more information, see Embedding models that support batch inference.
  • Processing Time: Batch jobs are processed asynchronously and are not designed for real-time applications. Most jobs complete within 24 hours after it starts running (not counting the queue time). After 24 hours, incomplete jobs are cancelled, and you'll only be charged for completed requests.
  • Canceled jobs: You can cancel batch inference jobs at any time. When you cancel a job, any remaining work is cancelled, and any already completed work is returned. You'll only be charged for the completed work.
  • Unsupported features: Batch inference doesn't support Provisioned Throughput, explicit caching or RAG. Batch inference implicit caching isn't supported in Gemini 2.0 Flash or Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite.
  • Image output: Batch inference is limited to the default 1K resolution. 2K and 4K outputs are not supported.
Note: Batch inference is not a Covered Service and is excluded from the Service Level Objective (SLO) of any Service Level Agreement (SLA).

Best practices

To get the most out of batch inference with Gemini, we recommend the following best practices:

  • Combine jobs: To maximize throughput, combine smaller jobs into one large job, within system limits. For example, submitting one batch job with 200,000 requests gives better throughput than 1,000 jobs with 200 requests each. Avoid jobs with fewer than 1,000 requests, because fixed per-job overhead takes up most of their run time.
  • Monitor Job Status: You can monitor job progress using the API, SDK, or UI. For more information, see monitor the job status. If a job fails, check the error messages to diagnose and troubleshoot the issue.
  • Optimize for Cost: Take advantage of the cost savings offered by batch processing for any tasks that don't require an immediate response.

What's next

  • Create a batch job with Cloud Storage
  • Create a batch job with BigQuery
  • Get batch embeddings inferences

Consumption options

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform offers multiple options for getting and using compute resources when using generative models. These consumption options are designed to meet the needs of any workload, from initial prototyping to production deployments. Selecting the right option is critical for balancing performance, reliability, and cost.

This guide details the available consumption options, helps you map them to your specific workload requirements, and provides strategies for optimizing latency, availability, and cost.

Consumption options

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides five consumption options tailored to different traffic patterns and business needs:

Consumption option Description Ideal for Pricing
Provisioned Throughput Provides guaranteed throughput for a commitment period Critical, steady-state, always-on workloads where an SLA is needed Commitment-based (available in 1-week, 1-month, 3-month, and 1-year plans)
PayGo Standard PayGo Flexible, pay-per-use option with no upfront commitment Default option for everyday use cases with flexibility for variable traffic demand Per-token (standard rate)
Priority Delivers higher reliability through priority processing while maintaining PayGo flexibility Important workloads that require higher reliability and limits than Standard PayGo Per-token (premium rate)
Flex Cost-effective option for latency-tolerant workloads Tasks that can tolerate slower response times and higher throttling in exchange for lower pricing Per-token (discounted rate)
Batch inference Cost-optimized for high-volume, asynchronous processing Large-scale jobs where results are needed within a longer timeframe Per-token (discounted rate)

For information on pricing, see the pricing page.

Choose the right option for your workload

The following sections provide guidance on selecting the most suitable consumption option based on your workload's specific requirements and characteristics.

Latency-sensitive workloads

Organizations often have to make tradeoffs between reliability and cost while choosing the right consumption models. While Provisioned Throughput offers the highest reliability, it can cause underutilization if your traffic has spikes. Similarly, PayGo might offer the maximum flexibility but cannot guarantee a quality of service. The following section describes how to best combine these mechanisms to achieve the optimal outcome:

  1. Cover baseline traffic with Provisioned Throughput. This improves utilization of your reserved capacity, making it economical while providing guaranteed reliability for the core of your traffic. To achieve this, do the following:
    • Analyze your minute- or second-level traffic patterns.
    • Determine the amount of traffic to be covered by Provisioned Throughput. It should cover your highest priority traffic.
  2. Manage spillover traffic with Standard pay-as-you-go or Priority pay-as-you-go: By default, traffic that exceeds your Provisioned Throughput baseline (called spillover traffic) is handled by Standard pay-as-you-go. If you observe higher variance in performance for requests above the TPM limit, you can mitigate that variance through optimization. Priority PayGo gives you the option to achieve reliable performance at a premium price, subject to the ramp limit.

Asynchronous, high-volume workloads

If you have a large backlog of requests (for example, if you have millions of documents to summarize), and immediate latency is not a concern, you should submit a batch job by formulating requests into a JSON file or spreadsheet. This is useful for use cases like image labeling, bulk document processing, or sentiment analysis on historical data.

This is the most cost-effective option for high-volume inference.

Latency-tolerant, cost-sensitive workloads

If you need to process requests where the application can wait for a response but cost reduction is a priority, you should use Flex pay-as-you-go. Flex PayGo offers reduced per-token pricing for requests that don't require immediate execution. This option is useful for use cases such as offline analysis, data annotation, product catalog building, or translation.

Optimization strategies

Once you have selected your consumption model, use the following strategies to further optimize for latency, availability, and cost.

Latency

When you build interactive applications, latency plays a crucial role in the user experience. Latency refers to the time it takes for a model to process your input prompt and generate a corresponding output response. When examining latency with a model, consider the following:

  • Time to first token (TTFT): The time it takes for the model to produce the first token of the response after receiving the prompt. TTFT is particularly relevant for streaming applications, where providing immediate feedback is crucial.
  • Time to last token (TTLT): The overall time the model takes to process the prompt and generate the response.

To optimize for latency:

  • Select the right model for your use case: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides a diverse range of models with varying capabilities and performance characteristics. Carefully evaluate your requirements regarding speed and output quality to choose the model that best aligns with your use case. For a list of available models, see Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden.
  • Reduce prompt size: Craft clear and concise prompts that effectively convey your intent without unnecessary details or redundancy. Shorter prompts reduce your time to first token.
  • Limit output tokens:
    • Use system instructions to control the length of the response. Instruct the model to provide concise answers or limit the output to a specific number of sentences or paragraphs. This strategy can reduce your time to last token.
    • Restrict output by setting a limit. Use the max_output_tokens parameter to set a maximum limit on the length of the generated response, preventing overly long output. Latency is directly proportional to the number of tokens generated; generating fewer tokens results in faster responses. However, be cautious as this might cut off responses mid-sentence.
  • Use Provisioned Throughput: For the most consistent performance, use Provisioned Throughput. This eliminates the variability caused by "cold starts" or queuing that can occasionally occur in PayGo models during high traffic.
  • Limit the thinking budget: If you're using a model that supports Thinking, you can reduce the latency by reducing the thinking budget. By limiting the internal reasoning tokens that the model generates before answering, you reduce the overall processing time. However, you must ensure the budget remains sufficient for the complexity of the task to avoid degrading answer quality.
  • Use streaming for your responses: Streaming enhances perceived responsiveness and creates a more interactive user experience. With streaming, the model starts sending its response before it generates the complete output. This enables real-time processing of the output, so you can immediately update your user interface and perform other concurrent tasks.

Availability

To optimize for availability:

  • Implement retry logic: Implement exponential backoff for 429 errors, particularly when using Standard PayGo.
  • Use a hybrid implementation: As detailed in Choose the right option for your workload, don't rely solely on PayGo for critical production apps. Combining Provisioned Throughput and PayGo provides the highest assurance against resource exhaustion (429 errors).
  • Manage your Provisioned Throughput quota: Regularly monitor your TPM consumption and increase PT GSUs before anticipated traffic events (such as product launches). You can use an alert policy to automate monitoring.
  • Use the global endpoint: Use the global endpoint to utilize Google's global capacity pool to minimize throttling due to regional capacity constraints.
  • Smooth your traffic to reduce spikes whenever possible: Higher PayGo traffic rates (TPM) tend to be associated with higher throttling rates.
  • Shift traffic to off-peak hours: Model usage in aggregate generally follows a diurnal pattern. Time-shifting your workload to off-peak hours or weekends can significantly improve availability.

Cost

To optimize for cost:

  • Right-size your Provisioned Throughput: You generally don't need to provision PT to cover peak demand. Provisioning for peak demand reduces overall utilization and drives up costs. Aim to cover a specific percentile of your traffic depending on your risk tolerance, and let Standard PayGo and Priority PayGo handle the rest.
  • Purchase longer-term Provisioned Throughput: A 1-year PT commitment is priced at a 26% discount compared to 1-month PT, leading to significant cost savings. You can always change the model associated with your purchased Provisioned Throughput GSUs to take advantage of our latest model capabilities.
  • Use Flex PayGo: Identify any part of your pipeline that is not latency sensitive (e.g., background summarization, data extraction) and move it to Flex PayGo to cut costs by ~50%.
  • Use batch processing: For asynchronous jobs such as processing large datasets, batch processing is significantly cheaper (50%) than processing requests sequentially using Standard PayGo.
  • Use context caching: Context caching helps reduce the cost and latency of requests that contain repeated content. Increase cache hit rates by placing large and common content at the beginning of your prompt, and sending requests with a similar prefix in a short amount of time.
  • Select a lower-priced model: If your use case allows for it, use one of our smaller models like Gemini Flash-Lite, which has a lower per-token price point than our heavy-duty, full-featured models.

Set up a Private Service Connect interface for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform resources

This guide shows how to set up a Private Service Connect interface for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform resources.

You can configure Private Service Connect interface connections for certain resources in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, including:

  • Ray on Vertex AI
  • Custom training
  • Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines
  • Agent Runtime

Unlike VPC peering connections, Private Service Connect interface connections are transitive. This requires fewer IP addresses in the consumer VPC network. This allows greater flexibility in connecting to other VPC networks in your Google Cloud project and on-premises.

This guide is for network administrators familiar with Google Cloud networking concepts.

Objectives

This guide covers the following tasks:

  • Configure a consumer VPC network, subnet, and network attachment.
  • Add firewall rules to your Google Cloud network host project.
  • Create an Agent Platform resource specifying the network attachment to use a Private Service Connect interface.

Before you begin

Use the following instructions to create or select a Google Cloud project and configure it for use with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and Private Service Connect.

  1. Sign in to your Google Cloud account. If you're new to Google Cloud, create an account to evaluate how our products perform in real-world scenarios. New customers also get $300 in free credits to run, test, and deploy workloads.

  2. In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project.

    Roles required to select or create a project

    • Select a project: Selecting a project doesn't require a specific IAM role—you can select any project that you've been granted a role on.
    • Create a project: To create a project, you need the Project Creator role (roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator), which contains the resourcemanager.projects.create permission. Learn how to grant roles.

    Go to project selector

  3. Verify that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.

  4. Enable the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Compute Engine, and Cloud Storage APIs, if any are not already enabled.

    Roles required to enable APIs

    To enable APIs, you need the serviceusage.services.enable permission. If you created the project, then you likely already have this permission through the Owner role (roles/owner). Otherwise, you can get this permission through the Service Usage Admin role (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin). Learn how to grant roles.

    Enable the APIs

  5. Install the Google Cloud CLI.

  6. If you're using an external identity provider (IdP), you must first sign in to the gcloud CLI with your federated identity.

  7. To initialize the gcloud CLI, run the following command: 

    gcloud init

  8. After initializing the gcloud CLI, update it and install the required components: 

    gcloud components update
gcloud components install beta

  9. In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project.

    Roles required to select or create a project

    • Select a project: Selecting a project doesn't require a specific IAM role—you can select any project that you've been granted a role on.
    • Create a project: To create a project, you need the Project Creator role (roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator), which contains the resourcemanager.projects.create permission. Learn how to grant roles.

    Go to project selector

  10. Verify that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.

  11. Enable the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Compute Engine, and Cloud Storage APIs, if any are not already enabled.

    Roles required to enable APIs

    To enable APIs, you need the serviceusage.services.enable permission. If you created the project, then you likely already have this permission through the Owner role (roles/owner). Otherwise, you can get this permission through the Service Usage Admin role (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin). Learn how to grant roles.

    Enable the APIs

  12. Install the Google Cloud CLI.

  13. If you're using an external identity provider (IdP), you must first sign in to the gcloud CLI with your federated identity.

  14. To initialize the gcloud CLI, run the following command: 

    gcloud init

  15. After initializing the gcloud CLI, update it and install the required components: 

    gcloud components update
gcloud components install beta
    16.
  16. If you're not the project owner and don't have the Project IAM Admin (roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin) role, ask the owner to grant you the Compute Network Admin (roles/compute.networkAdmin) role to manage networking resources. If you're only creating a network attachment in an existing VPC network, you can instead use a custom role that includes the compute.networkAttachments.create permission.
  17. Assign the required roles to the AI Platform Service Agent. For details about which roles to grant in different scenarios, see the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform service agent required role section of this document.

Set up a VPC network and subnet

Note: If you already have an existing VPC network, ensure the subnet IPv4 range is in the valid RFC 1918 ranges, and then go to the Create a network attachment section.

Follow the configuration steps to create a new VPC network if you don't have an existing network.

  1. Create a VPC network:

    gcloud compute networks create NETWORK \
    --subnet-mode=custom

    Replace NETWORK with a name for the VPC network.

  2. Create a subnet:

    gcloud compute networks subnets create SUBNET_NAME \
    --network=NETWORK \
    --range=PRIMARY_RANGE \
    --region=REGION

    Replace the following:

    • SUBNET_NAME: a name for the subnet.

    • PRIMARY_RANGE: the primary IPv4 range for the new subnet, in CIDR notation.

      The following are the IP requirements and limitations for Agent Platform:

      • Agent Platform recommends a /28 subnetwork.
      • The subnet of the network attachment supports RFC 1918 and non RFC 1918 addresses with the exception of subnets 100.64.0.0/20 and 240.0.0.0/4.
      • Agent Platform can only connect to RFC 1918 IP address ranges that are routable from the specified network.

      • Agent Platform can't reach a privately used public IP address or these non-RFC 1918 ranges:

        • 100.64.0.0/20
        • 192.0.0.0/24
        • 192.0.2.0/24
        • 198.18.0.0/15
        • 198.51.100.0/24
        • 203.0.113.0/24
        • 240.0.0.0/4

      For more information, see IPv4 subnet ranges.

    • REGION: the Google Cloud region where you create the new subnet.

Create a network attachment

In a Shared VPC deployment, create the subnet used for the Network Attachment in the Host Project, then create the Private Service Connect Network Attachment in the Service Project.

The following example shows how to Create a network attachment that automatically accepts connections.

   gcloud compute network-attachments create NETWORK_ATTACHMENT_NAME \
       --region=REGION \
       --connection-preference=ACCEPT_AUTOMATIC \
       --subnets=SUBNET_NAME

Replace NETWORK_ATTACHMENT_NAME with a name for the network attachment.

If the network attachment is created in a project different from the Service Project, you need to pass the full network attachment path when calling the Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform service agent required role

The Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform service agent (AI Platform Service Agent) requires specific IAM roles to manage networking resources and facilitate Private Service Connect (Private Service Connect) interface connections.

Depending on your network configuration, grant the following roles to the service agent (service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com):

  1. Compute Network Admin (roles/compute.networkAdmin)

    In the project where you create the network attachment, you must grant the roles/compute.networkAdmin role to the service agent. If you don't want to grant the roles/compute.networkAdmin role, you can create a custom role with the following permissions and grant it to the service agent:

    • compute.networkAttachments.get
    • compute.networkAttachments.update
    • compute.regionOperations.get

  2. Compute Network User (roles/compute.networkUser)

    If you are using a Shared VPC and you create the network attachment in a service project, grant the service agent (located in the service project) the roles/compute.networkUser role on the VPC host project.

  3. DNS Peer (roles/dns.peer)

    To enable resources like Agent Platform Managed Training or Agent Runtime to resolve private DNS records, grant the roles/dns.peer role to the service agent. Grant this role in the project where you are using the services. If using a Shared VPC, you must also grant the roles/dns.peer role to the service agent in the VPC host project.

Configure firewall rules

The system applies Ingress firewall rules in the consumer VPC to enable communication with the Private Service Connect interface network attachment subnet from compute and on-premises endpoints.

Configuring firewall rules is optional. However, we recommend that you set common firewall rules as shown in the following examples.

  1. Create a firewall rule that allows SSH access on TCP port 22:

    gcloud compute firewall-rules create NETWORK-firewall1 \
    --network NETWORK \
    --allow tcp:22

  2. Create a firewall rule that allows HTTPS traffic on TCP port 443:

    gcloud compute firewall-rules create NETWORK-firewall2 \
    --network NETWORK \
    --allow tcp:443

  3. Create a firewall rule that allows ICMP traffic (such as ping requests):

    gcloud compute firewall-rules create NETWORK-firewall3 \
    --network NETWORK \
    --allow icmp

Set up a private DNS peering

To enable Agent Platform Managed Training jobs or Agent Runtime agents configured with Private Service Connect interfaces to resolve private DNS records in customer-managed Cloud DNS zones, you can specify your network attachment and create private DNS peering while configuring or deploying your resource.

You can configure DNS peering by specifying target networks and domain suffixes in the dns_peering_configs field under psc_interface_config:

  • dns_peering_configs: A list of DNS peering configurations:
    • domain: The DNS name of the private Cloud DNS zone.
    • target_project: The project that hosts the VPC network. It can be different from the project where you created the network attachment.
    • target_network: The VPC network name in the target project to which the DNS peering is established.

For example, when creating a resource in Python, you can configure the private DNS peering as follows:

psc_interface_config = {
    "network_attachment": "NETWORK_ATTACHMENT",
    "dns_peering_configs": [
        {
            "domain": "DOMAIN_SUFFIX",
            "target_project": "TARGET_PROJECT",
            "target_network": "TARGET_NETWORK",
        },
    ],
}

Replace the following:

  • NETWORK_ATTACHMENT: the name or full path of your network attachment. For example, projects/SERVICE_PROJECT/regions/REGION/networkAttachments/NETWORK_ATTACHMENT_NAME. If you create the network attachment in a project different from the service project where you use Agent Platform, you must pass the full path of the network attachment.
  • DOMAIN_SUFFIX: the DNS name of the private Cloud DNS zone (for example, example.com.).
  • TARGET_PROJECT: the project that hosts the VPC network. It can be different from the project where you created the network attachment.
  • TARGET_NETWORK: the VPC network name in the target project to which the DNS peering is established.

Troubleshooting

This section covers some common issues for configuring Private Service Connect with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

When configuring Agent Platform with a Shared VPC, create the network attachment in the service project where you use Agent Platform. This approach helps prevent certain error messages, such as:

_Please make sure that the Agent Platform API is enabled for the
project_, by ensuring the
necessary permissions and APIs are enabled in the correct project.

  • Learn how to use Private Service Connect interface egress for Ray on Vertex AI.
  • Learn how to use Private Service Connect interface egress for custom training.
  • Learn how to use Private Service Connect interface egress for Agent Platform Pipelines.
  • Learn how to use Private Service Connect interface egress for Agent Runtime

Content Credentials

Content Credentials provide a transparent look into the origin and history of media files, for example, images, video files, audio files, and documents.

Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) is an open standards organization that has developed a technical specification for Content Credentials, called "C2PA metadata". This technology utilizes cryptographically signed metadata to provide secure and verifiable records of a media file's origin and any changes it's undergone. Being cryptographically signed, this information is tamper-evident, helping you verify the authenticity of the media asset.

Content Credentials include information about the creation process, the tools used, and edits that were made to a media file. For example, if you use an AI tool to generate an image, the Content Credentials will indicate that the image was AI-generated.

How to Use Content Credentials

If you generate a media file, such as an image, using a supported Google model, Content Credentials are automatically added and signed by Google LLC.

On the other hand, if you're viewing a file with Content Credentials in a C2PA-compatible application, you can view the file's history, such as the device, app, or service used to create and edit the file.

Note that C2PA doesn't classify media as "real" or "fake". It focuses on authenticating the source of the information and ensures that the content hasn't been tampered with. Even an AI-generated image is regarded as "authentic" if it has valid Content Credentials that describe how it was created or modified.

Moreover, C2PA doesn't guarantee the truthfulness of the assertions in the Content Credentials. The consumer of the media file is responsible for deciding whether the source or owner of file is trustworthy or not.

Verify Content Credentials

To verify the Content Credentials for a media file, go to the Content Credentials website. If the media file was created, edited, and published using only C2PA-aware tools, the Content Credentials are verifiable. Any modification to a C2PA-compliant media file using a non-C2PA tool is considered tampering, resulting in a validation failure.

Supported models

Content Credentials are supported by the following models. All images or videos created or modified using the listed models are automatically digitally signed by Google LLC. "Google Media Processing Services" is specified as the app or device used in the Content Credential.

  • gemini-omni-1.2-flash
  • gemini-omni-1.1-flash-preview
  • gemini-omni-flash-preview
  • gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image
  • gemini-3-pro-image
  • gemini-nano-banana-2.1
  • gemini-3.1-flash-image

Developer's guide to Gemini 4 Argon

Gemini 4 Argon is Google's frontier model that excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. It's the first model in the Gemini 4 family.

This document covers what's new with 4 Argon, the API conventions it enforces, how to migrate to it, and a quickstart. For an overview of the Gemini 4 family, see Get started with Gemini 4.

What's new in Gemini 4 Argon?

  • Unified input and output token limit: 4 Argon has a unified 1,048,576-token limit that includes both input and output tokens (where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response).
  • Long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens: Extends generation beyond the single-request output limit (65,536 tokens when streaming, or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming foreground requests) up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus your input tokens) on both the Interactions API and GenerateContent (v1beta1). The Google Gen AI SDK handles continuation_token automatically across segments, or you can run asynchronous server-managed background decodes (background=true) or manage continuation_token in a custom continuation loop.
  • Thinking levels: LOW, MEDIUM (default on gemini-4-argon), and HIGH (default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive).
  • Implicit caching with durable caching: Implicit caching applies automatically to shared prompt prefixes of 4,096 tokens or more, with durable caching enabled by default. Explicit context caching isn't supported.
  • Agentic video understanding: Generally available, and off by default.

Long decode examples

By default, a single foreground API segment generates up to 65,536 output tokens when streaming or 32,768 output tokens when non-streaming, where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response. To generate completions up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus your input tokens), use long decodes on either the Interactions API or GenerateContent. For continuation options, status transitions, and validation rules, see Long decodes.

Note: Known issue: Long decoding (continuation_token) on both the Interactions API and GenerateContent (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1) on Agent Platform. The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless you override api_version='v1'; for direct REST calls, use the /v1beta1/ endpoint path as shown in the following examples.

Use long decodes with the Interactions API

In google-genai >= 2.34.0 (Python), @google/genai >= 2.32.0 (JavaScript/TypeScript), Go >= 1.77.0, and Java >= 1.80.0, interactions.create() automatically follows continuation_token across segments whenever a segment returns status="requires_continuation". You can also opt out (automatic_continuation=False) to run a custom stored (store=True) or stateless (store=False) loop:

Python (SDK automatic)

from google import genai

client = genai.Client(
    enterprise=True,
    project="PROJECT_ID",
    location="global",
)

# Automatic continuation is enabled by default in google-genai >= 2.34.0.
# Unary calls merge all segments into one Interaction with summed usage.
interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    input="Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem.",
    generation_config={
        "max_output_tokens": 256000,
        "thinking_level": "high",
    },
)
print(interaction.output_text)
print(f"Merged segment IDs: {interaction.continuation_ids}")
print(f"Initial input tokens: {interaction.usage.initial_input_tokens}")

# Streaming yields events across all segments in order. Intermediate segments
# emit interaction.completed with status="requires_continuation".
stream = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    input="Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem.",
    stream=True,
    generation_config={
        "max_output_tokens": 256000,
        "thinking_level": "high",
    },
)
for event in stream:
    if event.event_type == "step.delta" and getattr(event.delta, "text", None):
        print(event.delta.text, end="", flush=True)
    elif (
        event.event_type == "interaction.completed"
        and event.interaction.status != "requires_continuation"
    ):
        print(f"\nFinal status: {event.interaction.status}")

# Optional: Delete each stored server segment before its 7-day TTL expires.
for segment_id in interaction.continuation_ids or [interaction.id]:
    client.interactions.delete(id=segment_id)

# Set automatic_continuation=False to return after a single segment.
single_segment = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    input="Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem.",
    generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 256000, "thinking_level": "high"},
    automatic_continuation=False,
)

Python (Custom loop)

from google import genai

client = genai.Client(
    enterprise=True,
    project="PROJECT_ID",
    location="global",
)

prompt = "Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem."

# Stored loop (store=True, default): chain previous_interaction_id + continuation_token
# without resending input.
segment = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    input=prompt,
    store=True,
    generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 131072, "thinking_level": "high"},
    automatic_continuation=False,
)
full_text = segment.output_text or ""

while segment.status == "requires_continuation" and segment.continuation_token:
    segment = client.interactions.create(
        model="gemini-4-argon",
        previous_interaction_id=segment.id,
        continuation_token=segment.continuation_token,
        generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 131072, "thinking_level": "high"},
        automatic_continuation=False,
    )
    full_text += segment.output_text or ""

# If status == "incomplete", max_output_tokens was exhausted; raise max_output_tokens to continue.
if segment.status == "incomplete" and segment.continuation_token:
    segment = client.interactions.create(
        model="gemini-4-argon",
        previous_interaction_id=segment.id,
        continuation_token=segment.continuation_token,
        generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 256000, "thinking_level": "high"},
    )
    full_text += segment.output_text or ""

# Stateless loop (store=False): resend original input + continuation_token
# with no previous_interaction_id.
stateless_seg = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    input=prompt,
    store=False,
    generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 131072, "thinking_level": "high"},
    automatic_continuation=False,
)
stateless_text = stateless_seg.output_text or ""
while stateless_seg.status == "requires_continuation" and stateless_seg.continuation_token:
    stateless_seg = client.interactions.create(
        model="gemini-4-argon",
        input=prompt,
        store=False,
        continuation_token=stateless_seg.continuation_token,
        generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 131072, "thinking_level": "high"},
        automatic_continuation=False,
    )
    stateless_text += stateless_seg.output_text or ""

import time
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(
    enterprise=True,
    project="PROJECT_ID",
    location="global",

interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    input="Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem.",
    background=True,
    store=True,
    generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 256000, "thinking_level": "high"},

from google import genai

client = genai.Client(
    enterprise=True,
    project="PROJECT_ID",
    location="global",
)

segment_id = None
checkpoint_token = None

stream = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-4-argon",
    input="Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem.",
    stream=True,
    store=True,
    generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 256000, "thinking_level": "high"},
    automatic_continuation=False,
)

try:
    for event in stream:
        if event.event_type == "interaction.created":
            segment_id = event.interaction.id
        elif event.event_type == "interaction.status_update" and event.continuation_token:
            # Checkpoints arrive at 32,768 output tokens and every 5,000 tokens thereafter
            checkpoint_token = event.continuation_token
        elif event.event_type == "step.delta" and getattr(event.delta, "text", None):
            print(event.delta.text, end="", flush=True)
        elif event.event_type == "interaction.completed":
            checkpoint_token = event.interaction.continuation_token
except Exception:
    # If the stream drops after a checkpoint, resume from checkpoint_token
    if segment_id and checkpoint_token:
        resumed_stream = client.interactions.create(
            model="gemini-4-argon",
            previous_interaction_id=segment_id,
            continuation_token=checkpoint_token,
            stream=True,
            store=True,
            generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 256000, "thinking_level": "high"},
        )
        for event in resumed_stream:
            if event.event_type == "step.delta" and getattr(event.delta, "text", None):
                print(event.delta.text, end="", flush=True)

Mandatory API rules and behavioral conventions

Important: Setting thinking_budget or thinking_level="MINIMAL" returns an HTTP 400 error. Valid values for thinking_level are LOW, MEDIUM (default on gemini-4-argon), and HIGH (default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive).

4 Argon enforces the conventions in the following sections for thinking levels, token limits, caching, generation parameters, and multi-turn tool execution.

Thinking levels

4 Argon supports three thinking_level values (thinking_budget and MINIMAL return an HTTP 400 validation error). The following table lists each thinking level and its recommended workloads:

Thinking level Recommended workloads
HIGH (default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive) Multi-file software engineering, formal proofs, architecture design, and vulnerability discovery.
MEDIUM (default on gemini-4-argon) General coding, tool use, document Q&A, and video understanding.
LOW Classification, summarization, and metadata extraction.

Token limits, caching, and billing

4 Argon applies the following token, caching, media, and billing rules:

  • Unified input and output token limit and single-request output limits: Token budgets and per-request limits work as follows:
    • The overall token limit of the model is 1,048,576 tokens and includes both input and output tokens (where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response). max_output_tokens controls the output token cap for the generation (up to 1,048,576 minus your input tokens); setting max_output_tokens greater than 1,048,576 returns an HTTP 400 error.
    • To avoid unintended long completions, the default single-request output limit (thinking + model response) is 65,536 tokens (or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming direct HTTP requests).
  • Long decodes: Single-segment foreground responses generate up to 65,536 output tokens when streaming or 32,768 output tokens when non-streaming. To extend single-turn output up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus input tokens) on the Interactions API or GenerateContent (v1beta1), see Long decodes.
  • Context caching: Explicit context caching isn't supported. Implicit caching (with durable caching enabled by default) applies automatically to shared prompt prefixes of 4,096 tokens or more, so put static content at the start of your prompt.
  • Agentic video: Uploaded videos default to media_processing="static". Set media_processing="agentic" to enable agentic video processing.
  • Token counting and billing: Every token the model processes is counted and billed, including thinking tokens and internal tool system instructions and function declarations when using grounding. Grounding with Google Search also remains billed per query.

Parameters, function calling, and chat validation

4 Argon enforces the following rules for generation parameters, tool calls, and chat history:

  • Ignored sampling parameters (temperature, top_k, top_p): The backend ignores custom values. Control reasoning depth with thinking_level, and output format with response_schema.
  • Unsupported parameters (frequency_penalty, presence_penalty, candidate_count): These return an HTTP 400 error. Remove them from your requests.

  • Function calling: Tool declarations and execution turns follow these rules:

    • Turn symmetry: Each FunctionResponse must match the id, name, and order of the preceding FunctionCall.
    • Sequential execution: Prefer sequential tool execution turns in multi-step tool loops.

    • Pre-tool formatting: Separate inline instructions with \n\n and avoid unstructured text before tool calls. To log intermediate state before a tool call, use a dedicated function declaration:

      {
  "name": "update",
  "description": "Update working notes before tool execution",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "OBJECT",
    "properties": {
      "previous_step": {"type": "STRING"},
      "plan": {"type": "STRING"},
      "next_step": {"type": "STRING"}
    },
    "required": ["previous_step", "plan", "next_step"]
  }
}

  • Chat sequence validation: Multi-turn chat payloads enforce the following constraints:

    • History payloads can't end with a model role turn.
    • Prefilled model turns aren't supported.

Long decodes

Long decode splits a generation up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus your input tokens) across multiple segments on either the Interactions API or GenerateContent (v1beta1). On the Interactions API, each foreground segment generates up to 65,536 output tokens when streaming (stream=true) or 32,768 output tokens when non-streaming (stream=false) and returns status="requires_continuation" with an encrypted continuation_token, or you can set background=true (store=true) so the server runs the continuation loop asynchronously and stores the merged output in one Interaction. On GenerateContent, streaming segments generate up to 65,536 output tokens and non-streaming segments generate up to 32,768 output tokens before emitting finish_reason=CONTINUATION with continuation_token, continuing until finish_reason=STOP. In Agent Studio, setting the output token limit greater than 65,536 up to 1,048,576 handles continuation tokens automatically. For runnable code samples, see the Long decode quickstart examples.

When to use long decode

Most requests finish within the per-request limit (65,536 tokens, or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming REST calls). Use long decode only when one response needs more output than that. Long decode gives the model more room to reason; it does not make answers longer (use thinking_level to control reasoning depth).

Workload Use long decode? Why
Hard math, science, research, and formal proofs Yes The model can spend more than 65,536 tokens to explore and check its reasoning.
The hardest coding and agentic tasks Yes Some tasks need more than 65,536 tokens of thinking and code in one response. Most coding and agentic tasks finish under 65,536 tokens.
Evaluation harnesses that stop at the output limit Yes Long decode prevents cut-off answers when the model spends an entire 65,536- or 32,768-token request on thinking.
Chat, Q&A, summarization, classification, and extraction No These tasks finish well under 32,768 tokens.
Requests for a fixed length, such as "write a 700,000-word book" No The model does not follow length targets.
Agents that call tools in many short turns No Each turn is short. Large outputs on each turn fill the unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit quickly.
Prompts near the 1,048,576-token input limit No Output can use only 1,048,576 tokens minus your input.
Latency-sensitive requests No Long decode can run for several minutes.

API version and SDK requirements

Long decodes require the following API version and minimum SDK versions:

  • v1beta1 API requirement (known issue): Long decoding (continuation_token) on both the Interactions API and GenerateContent (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1) on Agent Platform. The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is specified in http_options (or api_version="v1" on interactions.create); for direct REST calls, use the /v1beta1/ endpoint path.
  • SDK versions and OpenAI compatibility: For automatic continuation on the Interactions API, upgrade to Python google-genai >= 2.34.0, JavaScript/TypeScript @google/genai >= 2.32.0, Go >= 1.77.0, or Java >= 1.80.0 (for .NET and Kotlin on the Interactions API, use background=true or a custom continuation loop). For automatic continuation on GenerateContent, upgrade to Python >= 2.30.1, JavaScript/TypeScript >= 2.29.1, Go >= 1.74.0, Java >= 1.77.0, .NET >= 1.26.0, or Kotlin >= 1.6.0. Earlier SDK versions and the OpenAI compatibility layer cannot retrieve long completions using continuation tokens.

Interactions API continuation rules

The following status transitions, chaining rules, and storage behaviors apply to long decodes on the Interactions API.

Status values and output token budget

When generation_config.max_output_tokens is omitted on an Interactions API request, the total output budget defaults to 65,536 tokens (so a non-streaming call stops at 32,768 tokens with status="requires_continuation", and a second segment can generate the remaining 32,768 tokens). Set generation_config.max_output_tokens up to 1,048,576 (minus input tokens) for longer decodes in both foreground and background=true modes. The server returns the following status values:

  • requires_continuation: The per-segment output limit (32,768 non-streaming or 65,536 streaming) was reached before max_output_tokens; pass the returned continuation_token on the next request to continue decoding.
  • incomplete: The total max_output_tokens budget was exhausted; continuing with continuation_token without raising max_output_tokens returns an HTTP 400 error (max_output_tokens has already been exhausted). Increase max_output_tokens on the next request to resume decoding.
  • completed: Generation finished naturally and continuation_token is cleared.

Chaining, mode switching, and segment storage

Continuation requests on the Interactions API enforce the following rules:

  • Stored continuation (store=true, default): Pass previous_interaction_id set to the segment id that issued the continuation_token along with continuation_token, and omit input (the stored segment already holds the turn input). Always pair each continuation_token with the previous_interaction_id of the segment that issued it; passing a continuation_token on an already completed interaction returns an HTTP 400 error.
  • Stateless continuation (store=false): Omit previous_interaction_id and resend the original input alongside continuation_token on every segment.
  • Switching store modes across segments: You can switch from stored (store=true) to stateless (store=false) mid-decode by omitting previous_interaction_id and resending the original input with continuation_token. Switching from stateless (store=false) to stored (store=true) isn't supported because no stored parent interaction exists for previous_interaction_id.
  • Foreground and background=true mode switching and branching: Stored continuations (store=true) can switch between foreground (background=false) and background (background=true) execution across segments, including resuming a cancelled background=true interaction from its checkpoint continuation_token (persisted after 32,768 output tokens) in either background or foreground mode. Reusing the same previous_interaction_id and continuation_token creates independent branched continuations.
  • Turn-boundary enforcement: Starting a new user turn (previous_interaction_id with new input and no continuation_token) from a segment whose status is requires_continuation or incomplete returns an HTTP 400 error. Finish continuing the decode to completed, or branch your next turn from the most recent completed interaction. Once the final segment reaches completed, passing that final segment's id as previous_interaction_id reconstructs the full conversation history across all prior segments.
  • Parameter consistency across segments: Changing model, system_instruction, or function declarations (tools) on a continuation segment returns an HTTP 400 error. Keep thinking_level and built-in tools unchanged across segments as well (see Known issues).
  • Single-segment get, list, and delete behavior: In foreground mode (background=false), each segment is stored as a separate Interaction resource (interactions.get(id) returns only that segment, interactions.list() lists each segment separately, and interactions.delete(id) deletes only that segment). In the Google Gen AI SDK with automatic_continuation=True (stream=False), interactions.create() merges all segments on return and populates interaction.continuation_ids with the ordered segment IDs (ending with interaction.id). If a later segment fails or exceeds a numeric per-call timeout after earlier segments have completed, the SDK raises ContinuationInterruptedError carrying partial_interaction, continuation_token, interaction_id, and continuation_ids so you can resume from the last segment.

GenerateContent custom loop rules

In a custom GenerateContent continuation loop, follow these rules:

  • Set max_output_tokens greater than 65,536 (streaming) or 32,768 (non-streaming) up to 1,048,576, and resend the original contents, system_instruction, and tools on every continuation request along with the latest continuation_token (a top-level field on GenerateContentRequest in REST, or in GenerateContentConfig in the Google Gen AI SDK).
  • Don't append partial model output into contents or send a follow-up prompt asking the model to continue.
  • Continue looping as long as finish_reason is CONTINUATION and continuation_token is present, even if a segment spent all 32,768 or 65,536 tokens on thinking (parts: [{"text": ""}]). If finish_reason is MAX_TOKENS when continuation_token is present, raise max_output_tokens in the next request.
  • Combine accumulated parts into a single model turn for multi-turn history only after STOP.

Token counting, compaction, and implicit caching

Token accounting and caching across continuation segments work as follows:

  • On the Interactions API, non-streaming interactions.create() calls with automatic_continuation=True and server-managed background=true interactions sum token counts across all segments in usage (total_input_tokens, total_cached_tokens, total_output_tokens, total_thought_tokens, total_tokens), preserving the first segment's prompt count in usage.initial_input_tokens. In custom foreground loops and streamed interaction.completed events, each segment's usage reports only that segment's delta, so sum usage fields across segments for total billed tokens.
  • On GenerateContent, the Python Google Gen AI SDK (generate_content and generate_content_stream) accumulates total billed tokens across segments in the final usage_metadata and preserves initial_prompt_token_count. In custom REST loops, sum the final prompt_token_count, cached_content_token_count, candidates_token_count, and thoughts_token_count across segments.
  • Because each foreground continuation segment re-prefills the conversation and previously generated tokens as input, usage.total_input_tokens (on the Interactions API) and prompt_token_count (on GenerateContent) increase across segments. Don't use cumulative input counts to trigger context compaction in agent harnesses; instead, check usage.initial_input_tokens (or initial_prompt_token_count on GenerateContent) and compact only after the turn finishes (status="completed" or no continuation_token).
  • Each continuation segment re-prefills the prompt plus previously decoded tokens and automatically receives the 95% implicit context caching discount (4,096-token minimum) when segments run back-to-back within the 15 to 20 minute cache TTL. Completed segments are billed at the end of each segment even if a later segment fails or is cancelled.

Migrate to 4 Argon from 3.1 Pro

The following behavior is different from gemini-3.1-pro-preview:

  • 4 Argon has a unified 1,048,576-token limit across input and output (where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response), instead of separate input and output limits. Single-request output is capped at 65,536 tokens when streaming (or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming foreground requests), and can be extended up to 1,048,576 tokens using long decodes on the Interactions API or GenerateContent (handled automatically in the Google Gen AI SDK, with background=true on the Interactions API, or using continuation_token in custom loops).
  • thinking_budget returns an HTTP 400 error instead of being mapped to a thinking level. MINIMAL also returns an error.
  • Explicit context caching isn't supported.
  • Every token the model processes is billed, including internal tool system instructions and function declarations when using grounding.

For a side-by-side comparison, see Migrate from Gemini 3.1 Pro.

 client = genai.Client(
     enterprise=True,
     project="PROJECT_ID",
     location="global", # Supports "global", "us", and "eu"
 )

 response = client.models.generate_content(
-    model="gemini-3.1-pro-preview",
+    model="gemini-4-argon",
     contents=prompt,
     config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
-        temperature=0.0,
-        cached_content="projects/.../cachedContents/...", # Explicit caching unsupported
         thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig(
-            thinking_budget=16384, # Returns HTTP 400 instead of mapping silently
-            thinking_level="MINIMAL", # MINIMAL unsupported on Gemini 4 Argon
+            thinking_level="MEDIUM", # Valid: "LOW", "MEDIUM" (default), "HIGH"
         ),
     ),
 )

To migrate from gemini-3.1-pro-preview, do the following:

  1. Update the model ID to gemini-4-argon (or gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive for Fairwind-approved cybersecurity workloads).
  2. Upgrade to the latest Google Gen AI SDK and account for the unified input and output token limit: Upgrade to google-genai >= 2.34.0 (Python), @google/genai >= 2.32.0 (JavaScript/TypeScript), Go >= 1.77.0, or Java >= 1.80.0 for Interactions API automatic continuation (or >= 2.30.1 Python / >= 2.29.1 JavaScript on GenerateContent). Input and output tokens (including thinking and function calls) share the unified 1,048,576-token limit. For outputs exceeding 65,536 tokens (up to 1,048,576 tokens) on the Interactions API or GenerateContent, set max_output_tokens greater than 65,536 so the Google Gen AI SDK continues automatically across segments (or use background=true or a custom continuation_token loop).
  3. Replace the reasoning budget parameter: Replace thinking_budget and MINIMAL with thinking_level set to LOW, MEDIUM (default on gemini-4-argon), or HIGH (default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive) (use lowercase "low", "medium", or "high" on the Interactions API).
  4. Remove explicit caching and front-load static prompt content (4,096 tokens or more) for automatic implicit caching.
  5. Remove parameters that have no effect or aren't supported: Remove ignored and rejected generation fields as follows:
    • Remove temperature, top_p, and top_k, which are ignored.
    • Remove candidate_count, frequency_penalty, and presence_penalty.
    • Remove any prefilled model turns from conversation histories.

Summary checklist for developers

Known issues

The following known issues apply to 4 Argon long decodes:

  • Long decodes require v1beta1: Long decoding (continuation_token) on both the Interactions API and the GenerateContent API (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1) on Agent Platform. The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is set in http_options (or api_version="v1" on interactions.create); for direct REST calls, use the /v1beta1/ endpoint path.
  • Parameter changes across Interactions API continuation segments: Changing model, system_instruction, or function declarations across continuation segments returns an HTTP 400 error, whereas mid-decode changes to generation_config.thinking_level or built-in tools (google_search, code_execution, url_context) aren't rejected by server validation. Keep thinking_level and built-in tools unchanged across all segments of a continuation loop.

Supported models

The following tables show the models that support Provisioned Throughput, the throughput for each generative AI scale unit (GSU) and the burndown rates for each model.

Google models

Provisioned Throughput only supports models that you call directly from your project using the specific model ID and not a model alias. To use Provisioned Throughput to make API calls to a model, you must use the specific model version ID (for example, gemini-2.0-flash-001) and not a model version alias.

While Provisioned Throughput assures capacity for your model requests, it doesn't include or bypass quotas for other tools that you might use, such as Grounding. Depending on the size of your workload, you might need to request additional quota for these tools separately.

Moreover, Provisioned Throughput doesn't support models that are called by other Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform products, such as Agent Conversation on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and Agent Search on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. For example, if you make API calls to Gemini 3.5 Flash while using Agent Search, your Provisioned Throughput order for Gemini 3.5 Flash won't guarantee the calls made by Agent Search.

Provisioned Throughput doesn't support batch prediction calls.

The following is supported for Google models that support supervised fine-tuning:

  • Provisioned Throughput can be applied to both base models and supervised fine-tuned versions of those base models.

  • Supervised fine-tuned model endpoints and their corresponding base model count towards the same Provisioned Throughput quota.

    For example, Provisioned Throughput purchased for gemini-3.1-flash-lite for a specific project prioritizes requests that are made from supervised fine-tuned versions of gemini-3.1-flash-lite created within that project. Use the appropriate header to control traffic behavior.

Starting with Gemini 3, burndown rates for fine tuned model inference are higher compared to base model inference. This premium is proportional to the fine tuned inference premium for the model. For example, if fine tuned inference charges 50% more than base model inference, then the burndown rate for fine tuned inference would be 50% higher. In this case, if the base model inference of 1 input text token was 1 token, then the fine tuned model inference of 1 input text token would be 1.5 tokens.

Prior to Gemini 3, supervised fine-tuned model endpoints and their corresponding base model count towards the same Provisioned Throughput quota with the same burndown rates.

models/guides/gemini-3-6-flash:
Developer's guide to Gemini 3.6 Flash

Gemini 3.6 Flash is a high-speed, cost-effective powerhouse model in the Gemini 3 family. Designed to deliver near-Pro agentic capabilities without compromising on performance or value, the model is now generally available (GA) to developers using the Gemini API and for enterprises using Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

This document covers what's new with 3.6 Flash, how it fits within the Gemini model family, how to migrate to 3.6 Flash, and provides a quickstart for using 3.6 Flash.

How does it fit in the Gemini family?

Gemini 3.6 Flash is the primary agentic workhorse in the Gemini 3 family. It bridges the gap between deep-reasoning Gemini Pro models and high-throughput Gemini Flash-Lite models. Compared to Gemini 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash delivers significantly higher quality on multi-step tool orchestration, full-stack code refactoring, and visual reasoning while using fewer tokens and reasoning turns. It offers near-Pro level capabilities at Flash speed and pricing.

Model specifications and comparisons

The following table is a comparison covering some of the specifications between 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash, and 3.1 Pro:

Gemini 3.6 Flash Gemini 3.5 Flash Gemini 3.1 Pro
Model ID gemini-3.6-flash gemini-3.5-flash gemini-3.1-pro-preview
Launch stage GA GA Preview
Input types Text, Image, Audio, Video Text, Image, Audio, Video Text, Image, Audio, Video
Output type(s) Text Text Text
Context window 1,048,576 1,048,576 1,048,576
Maximum output token length 65,536 65,536 65,536
Supported regions Global, Multi-region Global, Multi-region, Americas, Europe, Asia Pacific Global
Supported thinking levels MINIMAL, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH
(Default: MEDIUM) 		MINIMAL, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH
(Default: MEDIUM) 		LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH
(Default: HIGH)
Primary focus High-efficiency agentic workflows, multi-step orchestration, and full-stack coding Balanced tasks, tool calling, and intermediate reasoning Deep reasoning, high-complexity tasks

See the 3.6 Flash model page for the full list of supported capabilities, tools, and consumption options.

What's new in Gemini 3.6 Flash?

3.6 Flash is optimized for multi-step orchestration, full-stack code refactoring, and general reasoning with significantly better token efficiency than its predecessors.

Capabilities and performance updates

The following is the list of changes in capabilities and performance for 3.6 Flash from preceding models:

  • Token and turn reduction: Consumes fewer tokens and completes multi-step workflows in fewer reasoning steps and conversational turns than 3.5 Flash.
  • Improved code generation: Produces cleaner code with lower compile-failure and revision rates across application building, prototyping, and IDE agent environments.
  • Reduced action bias: Resolves read-only diagnostic tasks without making unsolicited workspace edits or mutating state prematurely.
  • Multimodal and spatial reasoning: Delivers improved performance on chart interpretation, visual blueprint conversion, and multi-element web layout generation.
  • Computer use support: Supported as a built-in tool for agentic UI automation.
  • UI styling preference: Better at creating functional code, though human evaluators noted a preference for previous models for frontend presentation and visual layout. This can be mitigated by providing explicit design guidelines.

Behavioral and API parameter changes

The following is the list of behavioral and API parameter changes for 3.6 Flash from preceding models:

  • Step conciseness: Uses fewer reasoning steps than 3.5 Flash. While this reduces latency and cost on code refactoring and tool workflows, it can cause early exits on extended multi-turn conversational follow-ups where longer iteration chains are needed.
  • Upfront programmatic inspection: Prefers running diagnostic code scripts (execute_code) to inspect problems before mutating state more frequently than 3.5 Flash. While this improves diagnostic accuracy on complex backend refactoring, it can occasionally lead to running extra exploratory inspection steps on simple frontend web and scripting tasks where the previous version would generate code directly.
  • Default effort: Carries forward the medium default effort level introduced in 3.5 Flash.
  • No sampling overrides: Custom values for temperature, top-k, or top-p parameters are no longer supported. Setting custom values will be ignored in the API surface. Use thinking_level or structured JSON schemas to control output determinism instead.
  • Frequency and presence penalty restrictions: Custom values for these parameters are no longer supported. Setting them will now throw an active API error.
  • API requests where the last input turn has a role of "Model" are not supported.
  • Empty turns in conversation history are dropped.
  • Invalid thought signatures will now produce errors.
  • Strict function calling: FunctionResponse must strictly match the id, name, and execution count of the preceding FunctionCall. Append inline instructions directly inside the function response text, separated by two newlines (\n\n).

Quickstart

Before you begin, you must authenticate to Agent Platform using Application Default Credentials (ADC) or an API key. See Get started with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform for more information.

In the following code blocks, replace PROJECT_ID with your project ID.

Installation

Ensure you are using the latest google-genai SDK:

pip install --upgrade google-genai

Basic request

Python

from google import genai

client = genai.Client(enterprise=True, project="PROJECT_ID", location="global")

response = client.models.generate_content(
  model="gemini-3.6-flash",
  contents="How does AI work?",
)
print(response.text)

REST

curl -X POST \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/global/publishers/google/models/gemini-3.6-flash:generateContent \
-d '{
  "contents": {
    "role": "USER",
    "parts": { "text": "Why is the sky blue?" },
  },
}'

Migrate to 3.6 Flash from 3.5 Flash or 3.1 Pro

To migrate to 3.6 Flash from 3.5 Flash or 3.1 Pro, do the following steps:

  1. Update the model ID: Change model string in your API calls to gemini-3.6-flash.
  2. Adapt your code to the new Gemini 3 family API rules: Gemini 3.6 Flash strictly enforces the parameter rules and API conventions established across the Gemini 3 family:
    • Remove temperature, top-K, and top-P: Remove these custom parameters from your payload. While they won't throw an error, the model will ignore them entirely. Instead, use the thinking_level parameter or json_schema structured outputs to control output determinism.
    • Remove frequency and presence penalties: Remove any custom configurations for frequency or presence penalties to prevent your API calls from throwing runtime errors.
    • Ensure your chat integration does not attempt model prefilling: Review your message history arrays to ensure that your API payload does not end with an empty user turn or model turn.. If the last object in your history array is a "model" role (GenerateContent API) or "model_output" type (Interactions API), restructure the sequence to avoid triggering a strict validation error.
    • Use thinking_level: Remove instances of the deprecated thinking_budget parameter and use thinking_level instead.
    • Enforce strict function calling conventions: The FunctionResponse must strictly match the id, name, and execution count of the preceding FunctionCall. If you need to append inline instructions, place them directly inside the function response text separated by two newlines (\n\n).
  3. Account for workflow shifts:
    • If your application relies on multi-turn conversational loops, test your workflows to ensure the model's new step conciseness does not trigger premature exits.
    • If building frontend or basic scripting agents, monitor for unnecessary exploratory execute_code calls due to the model's new bias toward upfront programmatic inspection.

Workarounds for pre-tool text requirements

If your prompt requires the model to output structured text (XLM, YAML, Json, etc) (for example, <UPDATE>...</UPDATE>) immediately before making a tool call, the tool call may occasionally fail with a Malformed_Function_Call error. You can use one of the following workarounds to resolve this issue:

  • (Recommended) Instruct the model to put its pre-tool notes inside a dedicated update() function call instead of raw text. See the next section for detailed implementation instructions.
  • Instruct the model to write notes as Markdown headers (for example, # UPDATE, ## PLAN) instead of structured text.
  • Don't require the model to output text before tool calls.

Recommended solution: Wrap working notes in a dedicated function call

Instead of the original instruction:

Before calling a tool, in every response you MUST first output a single
`<UPDATE>` part as specified, don't skip this part or any of required sub-tags
within `<UPDATE>`.

Use this updated instruction:

Before calling any other tool, in every response you MUST first call `update`
with all required parameters (previous_step, plan, next_step, external).

Update all references to the old <UPDATE> XML format in the customer request. Then add the corresponding function declaration for the update function:

{
  "name": "update",
  "description": "Update working notes (previous step analysis, plan, next step, external note).",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "OBJECT",
    "properties": {
      "previous_step": {
        "type": "STRING",
        "description": "Key findings and outcomes since the previous step."
      },
      "plan": {
        "type": "STRING",
        "description": "The current status of the plan."
      },
      "next_step": {
        "type": "STRING",
        "description": "Brief explanation of the immediate next action according to the plan."
      },
      "external": {
        "type": "STRING",
        "description": "A short, plain-language note shown to the User about what you are ABOUT TO DO next."
      }
    },
    "required": [
      "previous_step",
      "plan",
      "next_step",
      "external"
    ]
  }
}

The model will make two calls in the same step: the update() call that replaces the structured XML, and the actual function call it wants to make.

Use Gemini Omni and references to generate videos

With gemini-omni-1.2-flash, you can generate videos from 3 to 15 seconds in length (3 to 10 seconds for preview models), specify generation_config.seed for reproducible results, and attach custom metadata labels (labels) to organize requests and track billing costs.

REST

Video generation can take over a minute to complete. You can choose from several interaction modes depending on your workflow:

  • Synchronous: stateless: Set store to false to generate a video in a single request without persisting the interaction state on the server.
  • Synchronous: stateful: Set store to true to persist the interaction state, which lets you retrieve the result later or reference the interaction ID for multi-turn video editing.
  • Synchronous: stateful streaming: Set both store and stream to true to receive model thoughts incrementally as they are generated, followed by the output video.
  • Asynchronous: Set background to true to run video generation in the background and retrieve the result later using the interaction ID.

Stored and asynchronous interactions are retained for up to 7 days.

For more information about using Gemini Omni models with the Interactions API, see Interactions API.

Synchronous: stateless

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_ID: A string representing your Google Cloud project ID.
  • MODEL_ID: A string representing the model ID to use. The following are accepted values:
    • "gemini-omni-1.2-flash"
    • "gemini-omni-1.1-flash-preview"
  • TEXT_PROMPT: The text prompt used to guide video generation.
  • CLOUD_STORAGE_IMAGE_URI: A string representing the Cloud Storage bucket that contains the input image. For example: "gs://video-bucket/input/".
  • IMAGE_MIME: A string representing an image MIME type. The following are accepted values:
    • image/png
    • image/jpeg
    • image/webp
    • image/heic
    • image/heif
  • CLOUD_STORAGE_VIDEO_URI: A string representing the Cloud Storage bucket that contains the input video. For example: "gs://video-bucket/input/".
  • VIDEO_MIME: A string representing a video MIME type. The following are accepted values:
    • video/3gpp
    • video/mp4
    • video/mpeg
    • video/quicktime
    • video/webm
    • video/x-flv
    • video/x-ms-wmv
  • CLOUD_STORAGE_OUTPUT_URI: Optional: A string representing the Cloud Storage bucket to store the output videos. If not provided, video bytes are returned in the response. For example: "gs://video-bucket/output/".
  • ASPECT_RATIO: Optional: A string representing the expected aspect ratio of the output video. If not provided, the aspect ratio is inferred from the prompt. The following are accepted values:
    • "16:9"
    • "9:16"
  • OUTPUT_RESOLUTION:

    Optional: A string representing the video output resolution. If not provided, the output defaults to 720p.

    gemini-omni-1.2-flash and gemini-omni-1.1-flash-preview support the following values:

    • "360p"
    • "720p"
    • "1080p"
    • "4k"

    gemini-omni-flash-preview only supports "720p".

  • DURATION: A string representing the length of the generated video files. Allowed strings are integers between 3 and 15 for gemini-omni-1.2-flash (or 3 and 10 for preview models), followed by "s" for seconds. For example, "10s" or "15s".

Use Veo and asset images to generate videos

Do the following:

Console

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Agent Platform > Agent Platform Studio page.

    Go to Agent Platform Studio

  2. Click Generate media.

  3. Click Video.

  4. In the Task menu, select Reference-to-video (Subject).

  5. In the Model menu, select a model from the available options.

    Note: veo-3.1-generate-001 only returns 8 second videos when you use subject images.

  6. In the Subject Images section, click Add.

    A file selection dialog is displayed. Choose one to three images on your computer to upload.

  7. Optional: In the Parameters section, adjust the following settings:

    • Aspect ratio: select either 16:9 or 9:16.
    • Number of results: adjust the slider or enter a value between 1 and 4.
    • Video length: select 8, 6, or 4 seconds.
    • Output resolution: select one of the following:
      • 720p
      • 1080p
      • 4k

  8. Optional: In the Safety section, select one of the following Person generation settings:

    • Allow (Adults only): default value. Generate adult people or faces only. Don't generate youth or children people or faces.

    • Don't allow: don't generate people or faces.

  9. Optional: In the Advanced options section, enter a Seed value for randomizing video generation.

  10. In the Prompt box, enter your text prompt that describes the videos to generate.

  11. Click Run.
