models/capabilities/inference-metadata-l:
Log inference request metadata

Agent Platform can write one structured log entry for every inference request your project serves. Each entry records metadata about the request: the model, the region, token counts (including input tokens, output tokens, cached tokens, thought tokens), Provisioned Throughput burndowns, end-to-end request latency, error code, and any header labels or request labels you attach. Entries go to Cloud Logging, and you can query them with SQL in Observability Analytics. To turn logging on, see Enable inference request metadata logs.

Inference request logging records metadata only. It doesn't record prompts or responses. If you need prompt and response content, use request-response logging instead.

This page describes how to enable inference request metadata logs, what each entry contains, and how to query them.

Use cases

Inference request metadata logs answer questions that aggregate metrics cannot:

  • Attribute token spend to a team, an application or a tenant, by attaching your own header labels, request labels or both to each request.
  • See which individual requests counted against your Provisioned Throughput quota and which were served on demand.
  • Break throughput, latency and error rate down by header labels or request labels.
  • Measure caching behavior per request rather than in aggregate.
  • Gain visibility into usage at second level, for example why a project received 429 errors, or why Provisioned Throughput spilled over. For the steps to resolve 429 errors, see Troubleshoot error code 429. To find the seconds that received them, see Error rate and latency by region.

Supported API methods for logging

Inference request metadata logs are supported for the following:

  • Gemini models that use generateContent or streamGenerateContent, including image generation through those methods.
  • Claude models that use rawPredict or streamRawPredict. Other partner models aren't logged. For Claude field names, see Token counts for Claude models.

Provisioned Throughput and every pay-as-you-go option are supported.

The following aren't supported:

  • chatCompletions.
  • embedContent, predict, and countTokens. Models that generate images through predict, such as Imagen, aren't logged.
  • Requests to fine-tuned models, including Gemini models tuned with supervised fine-tuning.
  • Tuning jobs, batch inference, and any other long-running operation.
  • Models that you deploy yourself in a custom container.
Note: Requests that the client cancels before completion don't produce a log entry.

Enable inference request metadata logs

You can configure inference request metadata logs for a whole project, or for a specific model in a specific region. If you need to enable at org level, please reach out to your account team. Logging configurations can take a few minutes to take effect.

Before you begin

  • Make sure you have the following IAM permissions on the project: aiplatform.endpoints.setPublisherModelConfig and aiplatform.endpoints.fetchPublisherModelConfig to change and read the setting, and logging.buckets.get, logging.buckets.list, logging.buckets.update and logging.operations.get to upgrade the log bucket. For predefined roles that include these permissions, see Access control and Access control for Logging.
  • Decide whether to upgrade the _Default log bucket to Observability Analytics. You need the upgrade to query entries with SQL or to view detailed metrics in the Google Cloud console. The upgrade takes several minutes and can't be undone. Entries written before the upgrade can't be queried with SQL afterward.
  • Review Cloud Logging pricing. Entries are stored for the bucket's retention period, 30 days by default, and Cloud Logging ingestion and storage charges apply. To estimate your cost, see Pricing.

Enable in the console

Enabling in the console turns on logging for every model in the project, both Gemini and Claude, on Provisioned Throughput and every pay-as-you-go option that the logs support. It also upgrades the _Default log bucket if it hasn't been upgraded. It sets the project-wide default described in Configuration precedence. Before you start, check the permissions and bucket upgrade.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Provisioned Throughput page.

    Go to Provisioned Throughput

  2. Do one of the following:

    • In the banner that reads Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is upgrading observability, click Enable.
    • In the toolbar, click Metrics settings. Select Enable detailed metrics, and then click Save.

  3. In the Enable detailed metrics? dialog, review the logging and bucket upgrade details, and then click Enable.

The dialog closes as soon as logging is on. The bucket upgrade continues in the background and can take several minutes. While it runs, the banner reads "Detailed metrics are on, and this project's _Default log bucket is being upgraded to Observability Analytics."

If the banner instead reports that the bucket hasn't been upgraded, click Upgrade to retry. If it reports that the bucket can't be upgraded, per-request logs can't be queried. Click Metrics settings and select Disable detailed metrics to stop the charges.

Note: The Enable and Upgrade buttons are unavailable if you lack the required permissions. To enable logging for one model or one region only, use the REST API. After you enable, verify that logging works, and then view detailed metrics.

Configuration precedence

Agent Platform resolves the setting for each request in this order:

  1. The per-model and per-region setting, if one is set.
  2. The project-wide default, if the per-model setting is unset.
  3. If neither is set, logging is off.

The per-model setting takes precedence over the project default. You can enable logging across the project and turn it off for one high-volume model in one region, or the reverse.

Enable with the REST API

You configure inference request metadata logs with the setPublisherModelConfig method, setting inferenceEventLoggingConfig.state to ENABLED.

Note: This configuration is available in the v1beta1 version of the REST API only.
Caution: When you set a per-model setting, send updateMask. If you omit it, the entire publisher model configuration on that model is replaced, which clears any request-response logging configuration already set on it. The project-wide call updates only the settings you include, so updateMask is optional there.

To set the project-wide default, address the project:

curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID:setPublisherModelConfig" \
  -d '{
        "publisherModelConfig": {
          "inferenceEventLoggingConfig": {"state": "ENABLED"}
        },
        "updateMask": "inferenceEventLoggingConfig"
      }'

To override one model in one region, address the publisher model:

curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL:setPublisherModelConfig" \
  -d '{
        "publisherModelConfig": {
          "inferenceEventLoggingConfig": {"state": "ENABLED"}
        },
        "updateMask": "inferenceEventLoggingConfig"
      }'

Set PUBLISHER to google for Gemini models and to anthropic for Claude models. For example, to enable logging for Claude Sonnet 4.5 on the global endpoint, use publishers/anthropic/models/claude-sonnet-4-5 with LOCATION set to global. For Claude model IDs, see Claude models.

The method returns a long-running operation.

Note: LOCATION must match the location of the model's endpoint. Publisher models served on the global endpoint require global. A mismatch returns INVALID_ARGUMENT and names the valid location in the error.

Get logging configuration

Read the current configuration with the fetchPublisherModelConfig method. Use the project to read the project-wide default, or a publisher model to read its override.

curl -X GET \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID:fetchPublisherModelConfig"

curl -X GET \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/PUBLISHER/models/MODEL:fetchPublisherModelConfig"

The response contains the settings that are set on that resource:

{
  "inferenceEventLoggingConfig": {
    "state": "ENABLED"
  }
}
Note: A setting that has never been written is absent from the response. An absent state, or a state of STATE_UNSPECIFIED, is treated as disabled.

Verify that logging works

  1. Send one request to a model you enabled.

  2. In Logs Explorer, run the following query. Most entries appear within 12 seconds; allow up to 5 minutes.

    logName="projects/PROJECT_ID/logs/aiplatform.googleapis.com%2Finference_request"

  3. To confirm that SQL works, open Observability Analytics and run any example query. If the query reports that the dataset wasn't found, the log bucket upgrade hasn't finished.

Disable logging

In the Google Cloud console, go to the Provisioned Throughput page, click Metrics settings, select Disable detailed metrics, and then click Save. This reverses Enable in the console.

With the REST API, follow these steps.

Disable logging by setting inferenceEventLoggingConfig.state to DISABLED on the same resource you enabled it on.

curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/PROJECT_ID:setPublisherModelConfig" \
  -d '{
        "publisherModelConfig": {
          "inferenceEventLoggingConfig": {"state": "DISABLED"}
        },
        "updateMask": "inferenceEventLoggingConfig"
      }'

Because a per-model setting takes precedence over the project default, disabling at the project level doesn't switch off a model that is explicitly enabled. Clear or disable the per-model setting as well.

Note: Disabling stops new entries. Entries already written stay in the log bucket until its retention period expires.

Where logs are written

Entries are written to the following log:

projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/logs/aiplatform.googleapis.com%2Finference_request

From there you have the standard Cloud Logging destinations:

  • Observability Analytics: Query the entries with SQL in Observability Analytics in the Google Cloud console.
  • Linked BigQuery dataset: Link a dataset to read the same data from BigQuery. For details, see Query a linked BigQuery dataset.
  • Aggregated sinks: Collect entries from every project under a folder or organization with a single sink. Filter on logName="projects/*/logs/aiplatform.googleapis.com%2Finference_request".

To collect entries from every project in a folder or organization, see Aggregated sinks overview.

Entries become queryable a short time after the request completes. Most entries are queryable within 12 seconds; allow up to 5 minutes.

Log entry schema

Each entry has two parts that you query separately: the monitored resource and its labels, which identify what served the request, and the JSON payload, which records what the request did. The following sections describe both.

Resource labels

For shared publisher models the monitored resource type is aiplatform.googleapis.com/PublisherModel, with the following labels.

Label Type Notes
resource_container STRING The project that served the request.
location STRING The region that served the request, for example us-central1. Requests sent to the global endpoint report global.
publisher STRING The model publisher, for example google or anthropic.
model_user_id STRING The model, for example gemini-2.5-pro.
Note: The location label reports global for any request sent to the global endpoint. To attribute throughput to a specific region, send requests to that region's endpoint.

Payload fields

Field name Type Notes
method ENUM GENERATE_CONTENT, STREAM_GENERATE_CONTENT, RAW_PREDICT or STREAM_RAW_PREDICT.
trafficType ENUM The consumption option that served the request. Current values are PROVISIONED_THROUGHPUT, ON_DEMAND, ON_DEMAND_FLEX and ON_DEMAND_PRIORITY. Absent on failed requests.
requestStartTime TIMESTAMP The time the serving frontend admitted the request.
requestDuration STRING End-to-end serving latency, formatted as a duration string such as 3.53s.
generateContentDetails.usageMetadata JSON Token counts for generateContent and streamGenerateContent, including per-modality breakdowns. Image output appears here as an IMAGE entry in candidatesTokensDetails.
rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata JSON Token counts for rawPredict and streamRawPredict, including partner models.
provisionedThroughput JSON Present for Provisioned Throughput traffic.
httpHeaders JSON Captured request headers.
error JSON Present only when severity is ERROR.
principal JSON The service account that issued the request, when available.
Note: A failed request records that it failed, not what it would have consumed. Both the trafficType field and the usageMetadata object are absent on error entries. You don't need labels to find spillover or downgrades: both are identified from successful entries, using the captured routing headers and trafficType. For details, see Identify spillover requests and Identify downgraded requests. Failed entries also capture the X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Request-Type and X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Shared-Request-Type headers you sent, so you can group failures by the consumption option you asked for.

The LogEntry.labels field carries gen_ai.operation.name, which follows the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. Both generateContent and streamGenerateContent report generate_content. Both rawPredict and streamRawPredict report raw_predict.

Provisioned Throughput fields

Field name Type Notes
ptChargedInputTokenCount INT64 Input tokens counted against your Provisioned Throughput quota, after burndown rates are applied.
ptChargedOutputTokenCount INT64 Output tokens counted against your Provisioned Throughput quota, after burndown rates are applied.
accountingResource STRING The project whose Provisioned Throughput commitment the request drew against.
Important: These counts are already adjusted for caching, modality conversion and burndown ratios. They are the authoritative burndown figures. Don't apply burndown multipliers to them a second time.
Note: These are quota counts, not billing amounts. Provisioned Throughput is billed by subscription, so these fields measure how much of your purchased throughput each request used.

Identify spillover requests

A request spills over when it was eligible for Provisioned Throughput but was served on demand because your throughput was used up. A spillover entry has a trafficType of ON_DEMAND and no provisionedThroughput object. An ordinary pay-as-you-go request looks the same, so use the following rules to tell them apart:

  • If you sent X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Request-Type with a value of shared, you routed the request to pay-as-you-go on purpose. It isn't spillover.
  • If you sent no X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Request-Type header, or a value other than dedicated or shared, and the entry reports ON_DEMAND, the request spilled over, provided that you have Provisioned Throughput for that model in that region.
  • If you don't have Provisioned Throughput for the model, every ON_DEMAND entry is ordinary pay-as-you-go.

For the header values, see Use Provisioned Throughput.

Note: The captured x-vertex-ai-llm-request-type header can hold more than one value. For Claude models, the platform adds a value of standard alongside the value you send. Check every value in the values array, not only the first.

For a query that counts spillover requests, see Spillover by minute.

Identify downgraded requests

A request is downgraded when you asked for one pay-as-you-go option and it was served on another. Compare the X-Vertex-AI-LLM-Shared-Request-Type header you sent with the trafficType that served the request:

Header value you sent trafficType when served as requested
priority ON_DEMAND_PRIORITY
flex ON_DEMAND_FLEX

Any other trafficType on a successful entry means the request was downgraded, or that the model doesn't offer the option you asked for. For a query, see Downgrades by model.

Error codes

Failed requests are written with a severity of ERROR and carry an error object with a gRPC status code and a canonical reason. The reason is a fixed string. It never contains prompt text, response text or your header values.

Code Status Typical HTTP status
8 Resource has been exhausted, for example a quota limit. 429
4 Deadline expired before the operation completed. 504
14 The service is unavailable. 503
13 Internal error encountered. 500
3 Request contains an invalid argument. 400
7 The caller doesn't have permission. 403
5 Requested entity was not found. 404

Attach custom header labels

To attribute usage to your own dimensions, such as a team, an application or a tenant, send request headers with the prefix x-goog-agent-platform-observability-label-:

x-goog-agent-platform-observability-label-team: payments
x-goog-agent-platform-observability-label-application: invoice-ocr

Each header appears in the entry under jsonPayload.httpHeaders. Header labels work on Gemini models with generateContent and streamGenerateContent, and on Claude models with rawPredict and streamRawPredict, on Provisioned Throughput and every pay-as-you-go option.

For example API calls with header labels, the log entries they produce, supported models, limits, and how header labels compare with request labels, see Custom metadata labels. To query them, see Usage by custom header label.

Query logs with Logs Explorer

Use Logs Explorer to find and inspect individual inference requests. It needs no setup beyond having logging enabled, and it reads the log directly, so entries are visible as soon as they arrive.

In the Google Cloud console, go to the Logs Explorer page and enter a query in the query-editor field using the Logging query language. For more information about the panes and controls, see Logs Explorer interface.

Start from the log name, which selects every inference request entry in the project:

logName="projects/PROJECT_ID/logs/aiplatform.googleapis.com%2Finference_request"

Add terms to narrow the results. Terms on separate lines are combined with AND.

  • To select requests served from one region, add resource.labels.location="us-central1".
  • To select one API method, add jsonPayload.method="GENERATE_CONTENT".
  • To select Provisioned Throughput traffic only, add jsonPayload.trafficType="PROVISIONED_THROUGHPUT".
  • To select quota errors only, add severity=ERROR and jsonPayload.error.code=8.
  • To select one custom header label value, add jsonPayload.httpHeaders."x-goog-agent-platform-observability-label-team".values="payments".
Note: A field name that contains hyphens must be quoted, as shown in the custom header label example.

Logs Explorer filters and displays entries. It doesn't aggregate them. To count, group or chart your entries, use Observability Analytics. In the Query results toolbar, click Analyze results to carry your current query across. That button appears only after the log bucket is upgraded.

Query and analyze logs with Observability Analytics

You can use Observability Analytics to query and analyze logs.

Before you begin

Observability Analytics answers questions that Logs Explorer can't. Logs Explorer finds and displays individual entries, which is what you want when you are chasing one request. Observability Analytics runs SQL across the whole set, so it can count, group, join and compute percentiles. Every question in this section needs aggregation: spend per team, burndown per project, and p95 latency per region can't be answered one entry at a time.

This requires the _Default log bucket in your project to be upgraded to use Observability Analytics. For more information, see Configure log buckets.

Important: Upgrade the bucket before you send the traffic you want to analyze. Entries written before the upgrade aren't backfilled and can't be queried afterward.
Note: The global in the table path is the location of the _Default log bucket, not the serving region. The bucket holds entries from every region. To filter by serving region, use resource.labels.location, as in Throughput by region and model. If your organization stores the _Default bucket in another location, replace global with that location.

The following examples run in Observability Analytics. Replace PROJECT_ID with your project.

Throughput by region and model

SELECT
  JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.location)      AS region,
  JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.model_user_id) AS model,
  JSON_VALUE(json_payload.trafficType)      AS traffic_type,
  COUNT(*)                                  AS requests,
  SUM(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.promptTokenCount) AS INT64))     AS input_tokens,
  SUM(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.candidatesTokenCount) AS INT64)) AS output_tokens
FROM `PROJECT_ID.global._Default._Default`
WHERE log_id = "aiplatform.googleapis.com/inference_request"
  AND timestamp > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 24 HOUR)
GROUP BY region, model, traffic_type
ORDER BY requests DESC

Provisioned Throughput burndown by project

SELECT
  JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.location) AS region,
  JSON_VALUE(json_payload.provisionedThroughput.accountingResource) AS pt_project,
  COUNTIF(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.trafficType) = "PROVISIONED_THROUGHPUT") AS pt_requests,
  COUNTIF(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.trafficType) = "ON_DEMAND")              AS on_demand_requests,
  SUM(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.provisionedThroughput.ptChargedInputTokenCount)  AS INT64)) AS pt_input_tokens,
  SUM(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.provisionedThroughput.ptChargedOutputTokenCount) AS INT64)) AS pt_output_tokens
FROM `PROJECT_ID.global._Default._Default`
WHERE log_id = "aiplatform.googleapis.com/inference_request"
  AND timestamp > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 24 HOUR)
GROUP BY region, pt_project
ORDER BY pt_input_tokens DESC

Usage by custom header label

SELECT
  JSON_VALUE(json_payload.httpHeaders
    ["x-goog-agent-platform-observability-label-team"].values[0]) AS team,
  COUNT(*) AS requests,
  SUM(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.totalTokenCount) AS INT64)) AS total_tokens
FROM `PROJECT_ID.global._Default._Default`
WHERE log_id = "aiplatform.googleapis.com/inference_request"
  AND timestamp > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)
GROUP BY team
ORDER BY total_tokens DESC
Note: A header name containing hyphens requires bracket notation. Dot notation doesn't work for these keys.

Consumed tokens per minute, Gemini and Claude side by side

This query reports consumed tokens per minute in one column per publisher. Each column weights token types the same way as the publisher/online_serving/consumed_token_throughput metric does for that publisher, so each column matches Cloud Monitoring. Gemini and Claude weight output and cache tokens differently, so don't add the two columns together. For the Claude fields, see Token counts for Claude models.

SELECT
  TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(timestamp, MINUTE) AS minute_ts,
  SUM(IF(JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.publisher) = "google",
    IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.promptTokenCount) AS INT64), 0)
      + IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.toolUsePromptTokenCount) AS INT64), 0)
      - 0.9 * IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount) AS INT64), 0)
      + IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.candidatesTokenCount) AS INT64), 0)
      + IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.thoughtsTokenCount) AS INT64), 0), 0)) AS gemini_consumed_tokens,
  SUM(IF(JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.publisher) = "anthropic",
    IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.input_tokens) AS INT64), 0)
      + 0.1  * IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.cache_read_input_tokens) AS INT64), 0)
      + 1.25 * IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.cache_creation_input_tokens) AS INT64), 0)
      + 0.75 * IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens) AS INT64), 0)
      + 5    * IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.output_tokens) AS INT64), 0), 0)) AS claude_consumed_tokens
FROM `PROJECT_ID.global._Default._Default`
WHERE log_id = "aiplatform.googleapis.com/inference_request"
  AND timestamp > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 24 HOUR)
GROUP BY minute_ts
ORDER BY minute_ts DESC

Cache hit rate across Gemini and Claude

Cache hit rate is cached input tokens divided by total input tokens. Gemini input includes tool-use tokens, because the cache can cover them. Claude input is uncached input plus cache reads plus cache writes. For how each publisher caches, see Context caching overview and Claude prompt caching.

SELECT
  JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.model_user_id) AS model,
  JSON_VALUE(json_payload.trafficType)      AS traffic_type,
  ROUND(100 * SAFE_DIVIDE(
    SUM(IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount) AS INT64), 0)
      + IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.cache_read_input_tokens) AS INT64), 0)),
    SUM(GREATEST(
          IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.promptTokenCount) AS INT64), 0)
          + IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.toolUsePromptTokenCount) AS INT64), 0),
          IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.generateContentDetails.usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount) AS INT64), 0))
      + IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.input_tokens) AS INT64), 0)
      + IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.cache_read_input_tokens) AS INT64), 0)
      + IFNULL(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata.cache_creation_input_tokens) AS INT64), 0))), 1) AS cache_hit_rate_pct
FROM `PROJECT_ID.global._Default._Default`
WHERE log_id = "aiplatform.googleapis.com/inference_request"
  AND JSON_VALUE(json_payload.trafficType) IS NOT NULL
  AND timestamp > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)
GROUP BY model, traffic_type
ORDER BY model, traffic_type

Downgrades by model

This query compares the pay-as-you-go option each request asked for with the option that served it. For how downgrades are identified, see Identify downgraded requests.

WITH entries AS (
  SELECT
    JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.model_user_id) AS model,
    severity,
    JSON_VALUE(json_payload.trafficType)      AS served,
    (SELECT LOWER(v)
     FROM UNNEST(JSON_VALUE_ARRAY(json_payload.httpHeaders["x-vertex-ai-llm-shared-request-type"].values)) AS v
     WHERE LOWER(v) IN ("priority", "flex")
     LIMIT 1)                                 AS requested
  FROM `PROJECT_ID.global._Default._Default`
  WHERE log_id = "aiplatform.googleapis.com/inference_request"
    AND timestamp > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)
)
SELECT
  model,
  requested,
  COUNTIF(served = CONCAT("ON_DEMAND_", UPPER(requested))) AS served_as_requested,
  COUNTIF(served IS NOT NULL
          AND served != CONCAT("ON_DEMAND_", UPPER(requested))) AS downgraded,
  COUNTIF(severity = "ERROR")                              AS failed
FROM entries
WHERE requested IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY model, requested
ORDER BY downgraded DESC

Spillover by minute

This query counts spillover requests per minute for each model that had Provisioned Throughput traffic in the window. For how spillover is identified, see Identify spillover requests.

WITH entries AS (
  SELECT
    timestamp,
    JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.location)      AS region,
    JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.model_user_id) AS model,
    JSON_VALUE(json_payload.trafficType)      AS traffic_type,
    EXISTS(
      SELECT 1
      FROM UNNEST(JSON_VALUE_ARRAY(json_payload.httpHeaders["x-vertex-ai-llm-request-type"].values)) AS v
      WHERE LOWER(v) IN ("dedicated", "shared")) AS routed_by_header
  FROM `PROJECT_ID.global._Default._Default`
  WHERE log_id = "aiplatform.googleapis.com/inference_request"
    AND severity = "INFO"
    AND timestamp > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 24 HOUR)
),
pt_models AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT region, model FROM entries WHERE traffic_type = "PROVISIONED_THROUGHPUT"
)
SELECT
  TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(e.timestamp, MINUTE) AS minute_ts,
  e.region,
  e.model,
  COUNTIF(e.traffic_type = "PROVISIONED_THROUGHPUT")              AS pt_requests,
  COUNTIF(e.traffic_type = "ON_DEMAND" AND NOT e.routed_by_header) AS spillover_requests
FROM entries AS e
JOIN pt_models USING (region, model)
GROUP BY minute_ts, e.region, e.model
HAVING spillover_requests > 0
ORDER BY minute_ts DESC

Error rate and latency by region

SELECT
  JSON_VALUE(resource.labels.location) AS region,
  TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(timestamp, MINUTE)   AS minute_ts,
  COUNT(*)                             AS total,
  COUNTIF(severity = "ERROR")          AS errors,
  COUNTIF(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.error.code) AS INT64) = 8) AS resource_exhausted,
  APPROX_QUANTILES(
    CAST(REGEXP_REPLACE(JSON_VALUE(json_payload.requestDuration), r"s$", "") AS FLOAT64),
    100)[OFFSET(95)] AS p95_latency_seconds
FROM `PROJECT_ID.global._Default._Default`
WHERE log_id = "aiplatform.googleapis.com/inference_request"
  AND timestamp > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 6 HOUR)
GROUP BY region, minute_ts
ORDER BY minute_ts DESC
Note: The requestDuration field is a duration string such as 3.53s. Strip the trailing s before you cast it to a number.

Token counts for Claude models

Claude models report usage under rawPredictDetails.usageMetadata, with the Claude API field names. Both rawPredict and streamRawPredict write the same fields; for streaming, the log merges the usage reported in the stream.

Field What it counts
input_tokens Input tokens that weren't read from or written to the cache.
cache_read_input_tokens Input tokens read from the prompt cache.
cache_creation_input_tokens Input tokens written to the prompt cache, both TTLs combined.
cache_creation.ephemeral_5m_input_tokens Cache writes with a 5-minute TTL.
cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens Cache writes with a 1-hour TTL.
output_tokens Output tokens, including extended thinking. Don't add thinking tokens separately.

Total Claude input is input_tokens plus cache_read_input_tokens plus cache_creation_input_tokens. Gemini differs: promptTokenCount already includes cached tokens.

Claude entries carry no modality breakdown. Header labels work the same way for Gemini and Claude; see Attach custom header labels.

Note: Calls to the Claude Count Tokens API appear as RAW_PREDICT entries with a model_user_id of count-tokens and no usage fields. Exclude them when you count requests.

Pricing

Inference request metadata logging writes to Cloud Logging and is billed as Cloud Logging ingestion and storage. Querying through Observability Analytics is billed as Cloud Monitoring usage. Linking a BigQuery dataset doesn't add BigQuery storage charges.

Entry size depends on your requests, for example on how many header labels they carry. To estimate your cost, enable logging for a representative workload for a day, measure the ingested volume with Log volume analysis, and then project your monthly volume in the Google Cloud pricing calculator.

What's next

  • Learn how to monitor models with metrics.
  • Learn how to monitor cost using custom metadata labels.
  • Use request-response logging if you need prompt and response content.
  • Read about Provisioned Throughput.
  • View detailed metrics for Provisioned Throughput in the Google Cloud console.
  • Troubleshoot 429 errors.
  • Collect entries from every project in a folder or organization with aggregated sinks.

models/tuning/text:
Text tuning

This page provides prerequisites and detailed instructions for fine-tuning Gemini models on text data using supervised learning.

Use cases

Fine-tuning lets you adapt base Gemini models for specialized tasks. Here are some text use cases:

  • Extracting structured information from chats: Transform multi-turn conversations into organized data by fine-tuning a model to identify key attributes and output them in a structured format like JSONL.
  • Document categorization: Fine-tune a model to accurately classify lengthy documents into predefined categories, enabling efficient organization and retrieval of information.
  • Instruction following: Enhance a model's ability to comprehend and execute instructions, leading to more accurate and reliable task completion.
  • Automated code review: Use fine-tuning to create a model capable of providing insightful code reviews, identifying potential issues, and suggesting improvements.
  • Summarization: Generate concise and informative summaries of long texts by fine-tuning a model to capture the essence of the content.
  • Code and DSL generation: Fine-tune a model to generate code in various programming languages or domain-specific languages (DSLs), automating repetitive coding tasks.
  • Improved RAG performance: Enhance the helpfulness and accuracy of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by fine-tuning the underlying language model.

Dataset format

The fileUri for your dataset can be the URI for a file in a Cloud Storage bucket, or it can be a publicly available HTTP or HTTPS URL.

The following is an example of a text dataset.

To see the generic format example, see Dataset example for Gemini.

{
  "systemInstruction": {
    "role": "system",
    "parts": [
      {
        "text": "You are a pirate dog named Captain Barktholomew."
      }
    ]
  },
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "Hi"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "Argh! What brings ye to my ship?"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "What's your name?"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "I be Captain Barktholomew, the most feared pirate dog of the seven seas."
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Sample datasets

You can use the following sample datasets to learn how to tune a Gemini model. To use these datasets, specify the URIs in the applicable parameters when creating a text model supervised fine-tuning job.

To use the sample tuning dataset, specify its location as follows:

"training_dataset_uri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/gemini-2_0/text/sft_train_data.jsonl",

To use the sample validation dataset, specify its location as follows:

"validation_dataset_uri": "gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/gemini-2_0/text/sft_validation_data.jsonl",

What's next

  • To start tuning, see Tune Gemini models by using supervised fine-tuning.

models/tuning/video:
Video tuning

This page provides prerequisites and detailed instructions for fine-tuning Gemini on video data using supervised learning.

Use cases

Fine-tuning lets you adapt base Gemini models for specialized tasks. Here are some video use cases:

  • Automated video summarization: Tuning LLMs to generate concise and coherent summaries of long videos, capturing the main themes, events, and narratives. This is useful for content discovery, archiving, and quick reviews.

  • Detailed event recognition and localization: Fine-tuning allows LLMs to identify and pinpoint specific actions, events, or objects within a video timeline with greater accuracy. For example, identifying all instances of a particular product in a marketing video or a specific action in sports footage.

  • Content moderation: Specialized tuning can improve an LLM's ability to detect sensitive, inappropriate, or policy-violating content within videos, going beyond simple object detection to understand context and nuance.

  • Video captioning and subtitling: While already a common application, tuning can improve the accuracy, fluency, and context-awareness of automatically generated captions and subtitles, including descriptions of nonverbal cues.

Limitations

  • Maximum video file size: 100MB. This may not be sufficient for large video files. Some recommended workarounds are as follows:
    • If there are very few large files, drop those files from including those in the JSONL files.
    • If there are many large files in your dataset and cannot be ignored, reduce visual resolution of the files. This may hurt performance.
    • Chunk the videos to limit the files size to 100MB and use the chunked videos for tuning. Make sure to change any timestamp annotations corresponding to the original video to the new (chunked) video timeline.
  • Maximum video length per example: Limit 1 video per example. It can be 5 minutes with MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH or MEDIA_RESOLUTION_MEDIUM and 20 minutes with MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW.
  • Dropped examples: If an example contains video that is longer than the supported maximum length, that example is dropped from the dataset. Dropped examples are not billed or used for training. If more than 10% of the dataset is dropped, the job will fail with an error message before the start of training.
  • Mixing different media resolutions isn't supported: The value of mediaResolution for each example in the entire training dataset must be consistent. All lines in the JSONL files used for training and validation should have the same value of mediaResolution.

Dataset format

The fileUri field specifies the location of your dataset. It can be the URI for a file in a Cloud Storage bucket, or it can be a publicly available HTTP or HTTPS URL.

The mediaResolution field is used to specify the token count per frame for the input videos. The following describes token counts for supported models:

  • Gemini 2.5:

    • MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW: 64 tokens per frame

    • MEDIA_RESOLUTION_MEDIUM and MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH : 256 tokens per frame

    Model tuning with MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW is roughly 4 times faster than the ones tuned with MEDIA_RESOLUTION_MEDIUM or MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH with minimal performance improvement.

  • Gemini 3:

    Token counts are the same as the base model. For more information, see Media resolution.

When a video segment is used for training and validation, the video segment is in the videoMetadata field. During tuning, this data point is decoded to contain information from the segment extracted from the specified video file, starting from timestamp startOffset (the start offset, in seconds) until endOffset.

To see the generic format example, see Dataset example for Gemini.

The following sections present video dataset format examples.

JSON schema example for cases where the full video is used for training and validation

This schema is added as a single line in the JSONL file.

{
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "fileData": {
            "fileUri": "gs://<path to the mp4 video file>",
            "mimeType": "video/mp4"
          },
        },
        {
          "text": "
          You are a video analysis expert. Detect which animal appears in the
          video.The video can only have one of the following animals: dog, cat,
          rabbit.\n Output Format:\n Generate output in the following JSON
          format:\n
          [{\n
            \"animal_name\": \"<CATEGORY>\",\n
          }]\n"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "```json\n[{\"animal_name\": \"dog\"}]\n```"
        }
       ]
    },
  ],
  "generationConfig": {
    "mediaResolution": "MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW"
  }
}

(Gemini 3 and later models only) Starting with the Gemini 3 models, you can also set the media resolution per individual media Part. This lets you mix resolutions in your dataset (for example, by setting MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH for one item and MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW for another). For more information about part-level resolution and their corresponding token counts, see Media resolution.

Part-level media resolution settings take precedence over global settings.

The following is an example dataset that sets the media resolution at both the Part and global levels:

{
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "fileData": {
            "fileUri": "gs://<path to the mp4 video file>",
            "mimeType": "video/mp4"
          }
        },
        {
          "fileData": {
            "fileUri": "gs://<path to the mp4 video file>",
            "mimeType": "video/mp4"
          },
          "mediaResolution": {
            "level": "MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH"
          }
        },
        {
          "text": "Describe these videos in detail."
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "Video 1 is low resolution while video 2 is sharp and clear"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "generationConfig": {
    "mediaResolution": "MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW"
  }
}

JSON schema example for cases where a video segment is used for training and validation

This schema is added as a single line in the JSONL file.

{
  "contents": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "parts": [
        {
          "fileData": {
            "fileUri": "gs://<path to the mp4 video file>",
            "mimeType": "video/mp4"
          },
         "videoMetadata": {
            "startOffset": "5s",
            "endOffset": "25s"
          }
        },
        {
          "text": "
          You are a video analysis expert. Detect which animal appears in the
          video.The video can only have one of the following animals: dog, cat,
          rabbit.\n Output Format:\n Generate output in the following JSON
          format:\n
          [{\n
            \"animal_name\": \"<CATEGORY>\",\n
          }]\n"
       }
      ]
   },
   {
      "role": "model",
      "parts": [
        {
          "text": "```json\n[{\"animal_name\": \"dog\"}]\n```"
        }
      ]
    },
  ],
"generationConfig": {
     "mediaResolution": "MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW"
  }
}

What's next

  • To learn more about video tuning, see How to fine-tune Gemini 2.5 using videos via Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

  • To learn more about the image understanding capability of Gemini, see our Image understanding documentation.

  • To start tuning, see Tune Gemini models by using supervised fine-tuning

models/gemini-use-supervised-tuning:
Tune Gemini models with supervised fine-tuning

This document describes how to tune a Gemini model by using supervised fine-tuning.

Before you begin

Before you begin, you must prepare a supervised fine-tuning dataset. Depending on your use case, there are different requirements for preparing a dataset:

  • Text tuning
  • Image tuning
  • Document tuning
  • Audio tuning
  • Video tuning
  • Tune function calling

To see an example of using the Google Gen AI SDK for Python to tune the text generation foundation model, run the "Supervised fine-tuning with Gemini for article summarization" notebook in one of the following environments:

Open in Colab | Open in Colab Enterprise | Open in Agent Platform Workbench | View on GitHub

To see an example of Supervised Fine-Tuning with integrated Gen AI evaluation service, run the "Supervised Fine-Tuning with integrated Gen AI Evaluation" notebook in one of the following environments:

Open in Colab | Open in Colab Enterprise | Open in Agent Platform Workbench | View on GitHub

Supported models

The following Gemini models support supervised tuning:

Click to expand supported models

  • Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite
  • Gemini 3.5 Flash
  • Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite
  • Gemini 2.5 Pro
  • Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite
  • Gemini 2.5 Flash

Create a tuning job

You can create a supervised fine-tuning job by using the Google Cloud console, the Google Gen AI SDK, the REST API, or Colab Enterprise.

Optional: (Preview) For Gemini 2.5 and earlier models, include the evaluationConfig to automatically run an evaluation using the Gen AI evaluation service after the tuning job completes. This evaluation configuration is available in the us-central1 region.

Console

Note: Creating a supervised fine-tuning job using the console is only available for Gemini 2.5 and earlier models.

To tune a text model with supervised fine-tuning by using the Google Cloud console, perform the following steps:

  1. In the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Agent Studio page.

    Go to Agent Studio

  2. Click Create tuned model.
  3. Under Model details, configure the following:
    1. In the Tuned model name field, enter a name for your new tuned model, up to 128 characters.
    2. In the Base model field, select the foundation model to tune.
    3. In the Region drop-down field, select the region where the pipeline tuning job runs and where the tuned model is deployed.
  4. Under Tuning setting, configure the following:
    1. In the Number of epochs field, enter the number of steps to run for model tuning.
    2. In the Adapter Size field, enter the adapter size to use for model tuning.
    3. In the Learning rate multiplier field, enter the step size at each iteration. The default value is 1. .
  5. Optional: To disable intermediate checkpoints and use only the latest checkpoint, click the Export last checkpoint only toggle.
  6. Click Continue.

    The Tuning dataset page opens.

  7. To upload a dataset file, select one of the following:
    1. If you haven't uploaded a dataset yet, select the radio button for Upload file to Cloud Storage.
      1. In the Select JSONL file field, click Browse and select your dataset file.
      2. In the Dataset location field, click Browse and select the Cloud Storage bucket where you want to store your dataset file.
    2. If your dataset file is already in a Cloud Storage bucket, select the radio button for Existing file on Cloud Storage.
      1. In Cloud Storage file path field, click Browse and select the Cloud Storage bucket where your dataset file is located.
  8. (Optional) To get validation metrics during training, click the Enable model validation toggle.
    1. In the Validation dataset file, enter the Cloud Storage path of your validation dataset.
  9. Click Start Tuning.

    Your new model appears under the Tuned Models section on the Tune and Distill page. When the model is finished tuning, the Status says Succeeded.

Python

Install the Google Gen AI SDK:

pip install --upgrade google-genai

To learn more, see the SDK reference documentation.

Set environment variables to use the Google Gen AI SDK with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform:

# Replace PROJECT_ID with your project ID, and set GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION to
# the region where the tuning job runs.
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=PROJECT_ID
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=us # Use us-central1 for Gemini 2.5 and earlier models
export GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE=True

Create the tuning job:

import time

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import (
    CreateTuningJobConfig,
    EvaluationConfig,
    GcsDestination,
    HttpOptions,
    Metric,
    OutputConfig,
    TuningDataset,
)

# TODO(developer): Update and un-comment below line
# output_gcs_uri = "gs://your-bucket/your-prefix"

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1beta1"))

training_dataset = TuningDataset(
    gcs_uri="gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/gemini/text/sft_train_data.jsonl",
)
validation_dataset = TuningDataset(
    gcs_uri="gs://cloud-samples-data/ai-platform/generative_ai/gemini/text/sft_validation_data.jsonl",
)

evaluation_config = EvaluationConfig(
    metrics=[
        Metric(
            name="FLUENCY",
            prompt_template="""Evaluate this {prediction}"""
        )
    ],
    output_config=OutputConfig(
        gcs_destination=GcsDestination(
            output_uri_prefix=output_gcs_uri,
        )
    ),
)

tuning_job = client.tunings.tune(
    base_model="gemini-3.5-flash",
    training_dataset=training_dataset,
    config=CreateTuningJobConfig(
        tuned_model_display_name="Example tuning job",
        validation_dataset=validation_dataset,
        evaluation_config=evaluation_config,
    ),
)

running_states = set([
    "JOB_STATE_PENDING",
    "JOB_STATE_RUNNING",
])

while tuning_job.state in running_states:
    print(tuning_job.state)
    tuning_job = client.tunings.get(name=tuning_job.name)
    time.sleep(60)

print(tuning_job.tuned_model.model)
print(tuning_job.tuned_model.endpoint)
print(tuning_job.experiment)
# Example response:
# projects/123456789012/locations/us-central1/models/1234567890@1
# projects/123456789012/locations/us-central1/endpoints/123456789012345
# projects/123456789012/locations/us-central1/metadataStores/default/contexts/tuning-experiment-2025010112345678

if tuning_job.tuned_model.checkpoints:
    for i, checkpoint in enumerate(tuning_job.tuned_model.checkpoints):
        print(f"Checkpoint {i + 1}: ", checkpoint)
    # Example response:
    # Checkpoint 1:  checkpoint_id='1' epoch=1 step=10 endpoint='projects/123456789012/locations/us-central1/endpoints/123456789000000'
    # Checkpoint 2:  checkpoint_id='2' epoch=2 step=20 endpoint='projects/123456789012/locations/us-central1/endpoints/123456789012345'

REST

To create a model tuning job, send a POST request by using the tuningJobs.create method. Some of the parameters are not supported by all of the models. Ensure that you include only the applicable parameters for the model that you're tuning.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • TUNING_JOB_REGION: The region where the tuning job runs. This is also the default region for where the tuned model is uploaded. For Gemini 3 and later models, use the us or eu multi-region endpoint.
  • BASE_MODEL: Name of the foundation model to tune.
  • TRAINING_DATASET_URI: Cloud Storage URI of your training dataset. The dataset must be formatted as a JSONL file. For best results, provide at least 100 to 500 examples. For more information, see About supervised tuning datasets.
  • VALIDATION_DATASET_URI Optional: The Cloud Storage URI of your validation dataset file.
  • EPOCH_COUNT Optional: The number of complete passes the model makes over the entire training dataset during training. Leave it unset to use the pre-populated recommended value.
  • ADAPTER_SIZE Optional: The Adapter size to use for the tuning job. The adapter size influences the number of trainable parameters for the tuning job. A larger adapter size implies that the model can learn more complex tasks, but it requires a larger training dataset and longer training times.
  • LEARNING_RATE_MULTIPLIER Optional: A multiplier to apply to the recommended learning rate. Leave it unset to use the recommended value.
  • EXPORT_LAST_CHECKPOINT_ONLY Optional: Set to true to use only the latest checkpoint.
  • TUNED_MODEL_DISPLAYNAME Optional: A display name for the tuned model. If not set, a random name is generated.
  • KMS_KEY_NAME Optional: The Cloud Key Management Service resource identifier of the customer-managed encryption key used to protect a resource. The key has the format: projects/my-project/locations/my-region/keyRings/my-kr/cryptoKeys/my-key. The key needs to be in the same region as where the compute resource is created. For more information, see Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
  • SERVICE_ACCOUNT Optional: The service account that the tuningJob workload runs as. If not specified, the Agent Platform Secure Fine-Tuning Service Agent in the project is used. See Tuning Service Agent. If you plan to use a customer-managed Service Account, you must grant the roles/aiplatform.tuningServiceAgent role to the service account. Also grant the Tuning Service Agent roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator role to the customer-managed Service Account.

HTTP method and URL: 

POST https://aiplatform.TUNING_JOB_REGION.rep.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/TUNING_JOB_REGION/tuningJobs

Request JSON body:

To create a model tuning job, send a POST request by using the tuningJobs.create method. Some of the parameters are not supported by all of the models. Ensure that you include only the applicable parameters for the model that you're tuning.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • TUNING_JOB_REGION: The region where the tuning job runs. This is also the default region for where the tuned model is uploaded. Multi-region endpoints aren't supported for Gemini 2.5 and earlier models. Use a regional endpoint, such as us-central1.
  • BASE_MODEL: Name of the foundation model to tune.
  • TRAINING_DATASET_URI: Cloud Storage URI of your training dataset. The dataset must be formatted as a JSONL file. For best results, provide at least 100 to 500 examples. For more information, see About supervised tuning datasets.
  • VALIDATION_DATASET_URI Optional: The Cloud Storage URI of your validation dataset file.
  • EPOCH_COUNT Optional: The number of complete passes the model makes over the entire training dataset during training. Leave it unset to use the pre-populated recommended value.
  • ADAPTER_SIZE Optional: The Adapter size to use for the tuning job. The adapter size influences the number of trainable parameters for the tuning job. A larger adapter size implies that the model can learn more complex tasks, but it requires a larger training dataset and longer training times.
  • LEARNING_RATE_MULTIPLIER Optional: A multiplier to apply to the recommended learning rate. Leave it unset to use the recommended value.
  • EXPORT_LAST_CHECKPOINT_ONLY Optional: Set to true to use only the latest checkpoint.
  • METRIC_SPEC Optional: One or more metric specs you are using to run an evaluation using the Gen AI evaluation service. You can use the following metric specs: pointwiseMetricSpec, pairwiseMetricSpec, exactMatchSpec, bleuSpec, and rougeSpec.
  • METRIC_SPEC_FIELD_NAME Optional: The required fields for your chosen metric spec. For example, metricPromptTemplate
  • METRIC_SPEC_FIELD_CONTENT Optional: The field content for your chosen metric spec. For example, you can use the following field content for a pointwise evaluation: "Evaluate the fluency of this sentence: {response}. Give score from 0 to 1. 0 - not fluent at all. 1 - very fluent."
  • CLOUD_STORAGE_BUCKET Optional: The Cloud Storage bucket to store the results of an evaluation run by the Gen AI evaluation service.
  • TUNED_MODEL_DISPLAYNAME Optional: A display name for the tuned model. If not set, a random name is generated.
  • KMS_KEY_NAME Optional: The Cloud Key Management Service resource identifier of the customer-managed encryption key used to protect a resource. The key has the format: projects/my-project/locations/my-region/keyRings/my-kr/cryptoKeys/my-key. The key needs to be in the same region as where the compute resource is created. For more information, see Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
  • SERVICE_ACCOUNT Optional: The service account that the tuningJob workload runs as. If not specified, the Agent Platform Secure Fine-Tuning Service Agent in the project is used. See Tuning Service Agent. If you plan to use a customer-managed Service Account, you must grant the roles/aiplatform.tuningServiceAgent role to the service account. Also grant the Tuning Service Agent roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator role to the customer-managed Service Account.

Colab Enterprise

You can create a model tuning job in Agent Platform by using the side panel in Colab Enterprise. The side panel adds the relevant code snippets to your notebook. Then, you modify the code snippets and run them to create your tuning job. To learn more about using the side panel with your Agent Platform tuning jobs, see Interact with Agent Platform to tune a model.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Colab Enterprise My notebooks page.

    Go to My notebooks

  2. In the Region menu, select the region that contains your notebook.

  3. Click the notebook that you want to open. If you haven't created a notebook yet, create a notebook.

  4. To the right of your notebook, in the side panel, click the Tuning button.

    The side panel expands the Tuning tab.

  5. Click the Tune a Gemini model button.

    Colab Enterprise adds code cells to your notebook for tuning a Gemini model.

  6. In your notebook, find the code cell that stores parameter values. You'll use these parameters to interact with Agent Platform.

  7. Update the values for the following parameters:

    • PROJECT_ID: The ID of the project that your notebook is in.
    • REGION: The region that your notebook is in.
    • TUNED_MODEL_DISPLAY_NAME: The name of your tuned model.

  8. In the next code cell, update the model tuning parameters:

    • source_model: The Gemini model that you want to use, for example, gemini-2.0-flash-001.
    • train_dataset: The URL of your training dataset.
    • validation_dataset: The URL of your validation dataset.
    • Adjust the remaining parameters as needed.

  9. Run the code cells that the side panel added to your notebook.

  10. After the last code cell runs, click the View tuning job button that appears.

  11. The side panel shows information about your model tuning job.

    • The Monitor tab shows tuning metrics when the metrics are ready.
    • The Dataset tab shows a summary and metrics about your dataset after the dataset has been processed.
    • The Details tab shows information about your tuning job, such as the tuning method and the base model (source model) that you used.

  12. After the tuning job has completed, you can go directly from the Tuning details tab to a page where you can test your model. Click Test.

    The Google Cloud console opens to the Agent Platform Text chat page, where you can test your model.

Tuning hyperparameters

It's recommended to submit your first tuning job without changing the hyperparameters. The default value is the recommended value based on our benchmarking results to yield the best model output quality.

  • Epochs: The number of complete passes the model makes over the entire training dataset during training. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform automatically adjusts the default value to your training dataset size. This value is based on benchmarking results to optimize model output quality.
  • Adapter size: The adapter size to use for the tuning job. The adapter size influences the number of trainable parameters for the tuning job. A larger adapter size implies that the model can learn more complex tasks, but it requires a larger training dataset and longer training times.
  • Learning rate multiplier: A multiplier to apply to the recommended learning rate. You can increase the value to converge faster, or decrease the value to avoid overfitting.

For a discussion of best practices for supervised fine-tuning, see the blog post Supervised Fine Tuning for Gemini: A best practices guide.

Evaluate the tuned model

If you didn't configure the Gen AI evaluation service to run automatically after the tuning job, you can interact with the tuned model endpoint the same way as base Gemini by using the Google Gen AI SDK, or by sending a POST request using the generateContent method.

Note: For global endpoint serving, the REST URL should use aiplatform.googleapis.com instead of the .rep.googleapis.com multi-region endpoint. Use the following endpoint format: 
https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/global/endpoints/ENDPOINT_ID:generateContent

For thinking models, we recommend setting the thinking budget to 0 (for Gemini 2.5 and earlier models) or the thinking level to MINIMAL (for Gemini 3 and later models) on tuned tasks for optimal performance and cost efficiency. During supervised fine-tuning, the model learns to mimic the ground truth in the tuning dataset, omitting the thinking process. Therefore, the tuned model can handle the task effectively without a thinking budget.

The following example prompts a model with the question "Why is sky blue?".

Console

Note: Testing tuned models using the console is only available for Gemini 2.5 and earlier models.

  1. To view details of a tuned model in the Google Cloud console, go to the Agent Studio page.

    Go to Agent Studio

  2. In the Tuned Models table, select Test.

    A page where you can create a conversation with your tuned model is displayed.

Python

from google import genai
from google.genai.types import HttpOptions

client = genai.Client(http_options=HttpOptions(api_version="v1"))

# Get the tuning job and the tuned model.
# Eg. tuning_job_name = "projects/123456789012/locations/us-central1/tuningJobs/123456789012345"
tuning_job = client.tunings.get(name=tuning_job_name)

contents = "Why is the sky blue?"

# Predicts with the tuned endpoint.
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model=tuning_job.tuned_model.endpoint,
    contents=contents,
)
print(response.text)
# Example response:
# The sky is blue because ...

REST

To test a tuned model with a prompt, send a POST request and specify the MREP_LOCATION and ENDPOINT_ID. For global endpoint serving, use the aiplatform.googleapis.com endpoint format described in the note above.

Before using any of the request data, make the following replacements:

  • MREP_LOCATION: The Google Cloud multi-region endpoint location that the tuning job runs in.
  • PROJECT_ID: Your project ID.
  • ENDPOINT_ID: The tuned model endpoint ID from the GET API.
  • TEMPERATURE: The temperature is used for sampling during response generation, which occurs when topP and topK are applied. Temperature controls the degree of randomness in token selection. Lower temperatures are good for prompts that require a less open-ended or creative response, while higher temperatures can lead to more diverse or creative results. A temperature of 0 means that the highest probability tokens are always selected. In this case, responses for a given prompt are mostly deterministic, but a small amount of variation is still possible.

    If the model returns a response that's too generic, too short, or the model gives a fallback response, try increasing the temperature. If the model enters infinite generation, increasing the temperature to at least 0.1 may lead to improved results.

    1.0 is the recommended starting value for temperature.
  • TOP_P: Top-P changes how the model selects tokens for output. Tokens are selected from the most probable to least probable until the sum of their probabilities equals the top-P value. For example, if tokens A, B, and C have a probability of 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 and the top-P value is 0.5, then the model will select either A or B as the next token by using temperature and excludes C as a candidate.

    Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses.

  • TOP_K: Top-K changes how the model selects tokens for output. A top-K of 1 means the next selected token is the most probable among all tokens in the model's vocabulary (also called greedy decoding), while a top-K of 3 means that the next token is selected from among the three most probable tokens by using temperature.

    For each token selection step, the top-K tokens with the highest probabilities are sampled. Then tokens are further filtered based on top-P with the final token selected using temperature sampling.

    Specify a lower value for less random responses and a higher value for more random responses.

  • MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS: Maximum number of tokens that can be generated in the response. A token is approximately four characters. 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60-80 words.

    Specify a lower value for shorter responses and a higher value for potentially longer responses.

HTTP method and URL: 

POST https://aiplatform.MREP_LOCATION.rep.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/MREP_LOCATION/endpoints/ENDPOINT_ID:generateContent

Copy a tuned model and serve in another region

To serve a tuned model on a global endpoint, copy an existing tuned model from a source region (such as us or eu) to the global region, create a global endpoint, and deploy the model to the endpoint.

For more information, see the Copy Model documentation.

Note: The global region does not support Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) and does not support Data Residency Zones (DRZ). Tuned model artifacts (adapters) for global models are stored in the US region because Cloud Storage does not offer a global bucket location.

The following REST command examples demonstrate how to copy a model to the global region, create a global endpoint, and deploy the model:

  • Copy Model to Global Region:

    curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \
     -d '{
        "sourceModel": "projects/SRC_PROJECT_ID/locations/SRC_LOCATION/models/MODEL_ID"
      }' \
     "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/global/models:copy"

  • Create Global Endpoint:

    curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/global/endpoints" \
     -d '{
       "displayName": "tuned_global_endpoint"
     }'

  • Deploy Model to Global Endpoint:

    curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/global/endpoints/ENDPOINT_ID:deployModel" \
     -d '{
       "deployedModel": {
         "model": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/global/models/MODEL_ID",
         "displayName": "tuned_deploy_model",
         "automaticResources": {"minReplicaCount": 1, "maxReplicaCount": 1}
       }
     }'

Tuning and validation metrics

You can configure a model tuning job to collect and report model tuning and model evaluation metrics, which can then be visualized in Agent Studio.

Note: Viewing tuning metrics using the console is only available for Gemini 2.5 and earlier models.

  1. To view details of a tuned model in the Google Cloud console, go to the Agent Studio page.

    Go to Agent Studio

  2. In the Tune and Distill table, click the name of the tuned model that you want to view metrics for.

    The tuning metrics appear under the Monitor tab.

Model tuning metrics

The model tuning job automatically collects the following tuning metrics for the model:

  • /train_total_loss: Loss for the tuning dataset at a training step.
  • /train_fraction_of_correct_next_step_preds: The token accuracy at a training step. A single inference consists of a sequence of predicted tokens. This metric measures the accuracy of the predicted tokens when compared to the ground truth in the tuning dataset.
  • /train_num_predictions: Number of predicted tokens at a training step.

Model validation metrics

You can configure a model tuning job to collect the following validation metrics for the model:

  • /eval_total_loss: Loss for the validation dataset at a validation step.
  • /eval_fraction_of_correct_next_step_preds: The token accuracy at a validation step. A single inference consists of a sequence of predicted tokens. This metric measures the accuracy of the predicted tokens when compared to the ground truth in the validation dataset.
  • /eval_num_predictions: Number of predicted tokens at a validation step.

The metrics visualizations are available after the tuning job starts running. It will be updated in real time as tuning progresses. If you don't specify a validation dataset when you create the tuning job, only the visualizations for the tuning metrics are available.

models/model-observability:
Monitor models

This document explains how to monitor the behavior, health, and performance of your fully-managed models in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It describes how to use the prebuilt model observability dashboard to gain insights into model usage, identify latency issues, and troubleshoot errors.

You learn how to do the following:

  • Access and interpret the model observability dashboard.
  • View available monitoring metrics.
  • Monitor model endpoint traffic using Metrics Explorer.

Access and interpret the model observability dashboard

Agent Platform provides a prebuilt model observability dashboard to view the behavior, health, and performance of fully-managed models. Fully-managed models, also known as Model as a Service (MaaS), are provided by Google and include Google's Gemini models and partner models with managed endpoints. Metrics from self-hosted models aren't included in the dashboard.

Agent Platform automatically collects and reports activity from MaaS models to help you quickly troubleshoot latency issues and monitor capacity.

Use case

As an application developer, you can view how your users are interacting with the models that you've exposed. For example, you can view how model usage (model requests per second) and the compute intensity of user prompts (model invocation latencies) are trending over time. Consequently, because these metrics are related to model usage, you can also estimate costs for running each model.

When an issue arises, you can quickly troubleshoot from the dashboard. You can check if models are responding reliably and in a timely manner by viewing API error rates, first token latencies, and token throughput.

Available monitoring metrics

The model observability dashboard displays a subset of metrics that are collected by Cloud Monitoring, such as model request per second (QPS), token throughput, and first token latencies. View the dashboard to see all the available metrics.

Limitations

Agent Platform captures dashboard metrics only for API calls to a model's endpoint. Google Cloud console usage, such as metrics from Agent Studio, aren't added to the dashboard.

View the dashboard

  1. In the Agent Platform section of the Google Cloud console, go to the Dashboard page.

Go to Agent Platform 1. In the dashboard, under Model observability, click Show all metrics to view the model observability dashboard in the Google Cloud Observability console.

Note: The observability section is available only if you or another user has made API calls to a MaaS model in your project.

  1. To view metrics for a specific model or in a particular location, set one or more filters at the top of the dashboard page.

    For descriptions of each metric, see the "aiplatform" section on the Google Cloud metrics page.

View 1-second resolution

The model observability dashboard adds 1-second resolution options to its existing charts when inference request metadata logging is on. The 1-second options read inference request metadata logs instead of one-minute aggregate metrics, so they show bursts that a one-minute average hides.

The 1-second options need inference request metadata logging on the project and a _Default log bucket upgraded to Observability Analytics. To turn on logging, see Enable inference request metadata logs.

Note: Inference request metadata logging covers Gemini and Claude models, on Provisioned Throughput and every pay-as-you-go option that the logs support. Cloud Logging charges apply.

To view them, click Show all metrics to open the model observability dashboard. Charts that support 1-second resolution have a drop-down in their header: Model requests per second (QPS), Token count by model, Model invocations by response code, Model invocations error rate (%), and the charts in the Tokens section. Each drop-down keeps the existing 1-minute resolution from metrics option as the default and adds a 1-second resolution from logs option. Select the 1-second option and set the time range to 200 seconds or less to see one point per second; at longer ranges, each point is the average per second in its bucket. Until logging is on, the 1-second options show "No inference request logs in this window. Turn on logging to see 1-second data." in the chart legend, and the 1-minute options work as before.

Monitor model endpoint traffic

Use the following instructions to monitor traffic to your endpoint in the Metrics Explorer.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Metrics Explorer page.

    Go to Metrics Explorer

  2. Select the project you want to view metrics for.
